THE MOTHERLESS TURKEYS. The white Turkey was dead ! the white Turkey was

dead! Howthe news through the barnyard vrap flying. Of a mother bereft, four small turkeys were left, And their case for assistance was crying. E'en the Peacock respectfully folded his tail, As a suitable symbol of sorrow; And his plainer wife said, "Now the old bird is dead, Who will tend the poor chicks on the morrow ? And when everting around them comes dreary and chill, Who albout them will watchfully hover ?" "Two each night will I tuck 'neath my wing," said the Duck, • "Though I've eight of my own I must cover." "I've too much to do; for the beetles and worms, In the garden 'tis tiresome pickin', I have nothing to spare, for my own I must care," 77' Said the Hen with one chicken. , "How I wish," said the Goose, "I could be of some use, For my heart is with love over-brimming; The next morning that's fine they shall go with my nine Little yellow-backed goslings out swimming." "I will do what I can," the old Dorking began, "And for help they may call upon me too; Though I've ten of my own that are only half grown, And a great deal of trouble to see to. But those poor little things, they are all heads and wings, And th'eir bones through their feathers are stickin'." "Very hard it may be, but, oh! don't come to me ! " Said the Hen with ore chicken. :Half my care, I suppose, there is nobody knows; I'm the most over-burdened of mothers; They must learn, the young° elves, how to scratch for themselves, And not-seek to depend upon others." She went by with a cluck, aud the Goose to the Duck Exclaimed in surprise, " Wel). I never !" Said the Duck." I declare, those that nave the least care, You will find are complaining for ever." So when all things appear to look threatening and drear, And when troubles your pathway are thick in, For aid in yew woe, oh, beware Low you ge To the Hen with one chicken!

Ax Amsrarra SP.ORTSMAN.—The meanest man on record lives in the Rappahanock Valley. • When one of his children falls downstairs he whips it for crying. One day last , summer a party of tourists stopped at his place, and he sent his boy Zeph out to hunt scjOirrels to make them a squirrel pie. He gave Zeph twelve pebbles with which he was to kill the game. When the boy returned he had eleven squirrels tied in a bunch. " Whar's the t'other one of,the dozen ? "asked the old man. "Missed him." "What's the pebble, you lazy son of a gun?" "-L-o-o-st it," sobbed the boys beggining to blubber. "I'll gin ve suthin' to remember it by," said the old man, and he laid on till the company made him desist. The boy had his share of the pot pie notwithstanding. RELATIONS.—A peasant took a fowl to his curd. The pastor kept him to dinner. A week later another peasant called at the manse; this time with empty hands. "Who are you, and what have you come fore "Mon- sieur Is Cure, I am the brotherof the man wt•o gave you a fowl." SS rake a seat." Day after day a whole string of cousins, neighbours. &c., dropped in at meal-times to. •eat soup" at the manse, until at last the mire, tired of this sort of thing, ordered his cook to place a large bowl "of hot water before the next visitor, who was none other than "a relative of the cousin of the nephew of the brother-in-law of the brother of the man with the fowl." Be pulled a wry face. "What's this?" he said to the cook. "That's the relative ot the cousin of the nephew of Vie,Prother-in-law °Lille brother of the broth of the fowl." UNCOMMONLY DEAF.—A rancid-looking old fellow was curled up in a corner of a Woodward-a Venue car the other day when a dudish-appearing young chap came in and took a seat beside him. The old fellow looked him over in a disgusted way, and it was plain enough that he wanted to pick a fight. The opportunity soon came. The dude, in moving about, touched the other's foot, and Promptly said—" Beg pardon, sir." "How!" called the other, as The put his hand to his ear. "Beg pardon !" " How ! What is it?" roared the other. "I beg your pardon, sir!" "A beggar, eh No, sir, I have nothing to give beggars! Why don't you go to work?" "1 sal I begged your pardon!" shouted the dude, as his face grew riflery, red. " NPt a ceet ! " screamed the old man, - as he waved his arms around. "You are just as well able to work as I am, and you ought to be pulled in for begging! Who are you, and where do you live?" The dude couldn't stand any more. The passengers were all laughing, and he rose up and made a sneak off the car. " He simply begged your pardon," explained a man across the aisle. "Exactly!" whispered the old man, "but I didn't want my pardon begged. My pardon is all right. He should have come down town in a dog-cart." A NURSERY roll SAILOI2S.—But the fame of Poole, during the fifteenth and two following centuries, was more by sea than by land: The mad' creeks 'which pierce the margin of its harbour render concealm-nt for a small vfellsel easy, and approach, even if it be dis- covered, difficult for an assailant. Thus there was on the coasts of Poole commerce not seldom other than legitimate, and it became a nursery in which a number of sailors were bred, who, in time of war, Ook to pri- vateering. The more noted among these is &certain Henry Paget whose name was generally corrupted into Arrinay. His ves=el harassed the coasts of France and of ppain to such an extent that no prize could pass along the channel of Flanders without being taken; and even Finisterre was plundered by h;s marauders. At last the two kings determined to retaliate, and to crush this wasp's nest; so a joint expedition was fitted oat., which advanted along the southern coast, plundering" and burning as opportunity offered. At Poole they landed, and the townsmen came out bravely to do them bailie. The invaders were, however, too strong', and the defenders had to retreat with heavy loss within their trenches, after which the assailants returned to their' ships and sailed away. At a later date other valiant deeds are recorded of the me. f Poole. "In 1694 Peter Jolliffe, captain of a small brig, attacked a French pri- vateer three times his strength„which had captured all English fishing-boat off Weymouth, forced her to give up her prize, and drove her ashore, near Lulworth. • For this exploit he received a gold chain and medal fromd William 111. The next year William Thompson, master a'fishing-hoat. with only a man and a boy, got the better of a privateer of Cherbourg with sixteen men. which was preparing to attack him, and brought her safely into Poole harbour, receiving also a gold chain and a gold medal from tha Lords of the Admiralty, Novem- ber 5, 1797, the brig General Wolfe, of Pe, having been taken by a French priYateer, the mate, his man, and a boy rose against their captors, overpowered them, and brought the brig into Cork harbour."—Our Own Counba4 ESSAY ON NEWSPAPERS.—The souvenir darling orders of the Albany Printing Pressmen's Union contain the following contribution from "a printer's devil," which is too funny for pablication in so-called comic papers; at least, they seldom have such genuine humour. It is en- titled a " Prize Essay on :Newspapers" :—NewSpapers is called vehicles of information._ -Reporters is what is

called "the staff "—so many of them being "sticks:' They work hard—at refreshment bars. Proof-readers is men what poils the punctuation of crympositors. They ' spell. a word one way to-day, and another way to- morrow. They think they be intelligent persons; corn- pdsitors think different. Cympositors is men as sets up the type—and sometimes they drinks. Compositors is very steady men when they is sober—which they seldom is when they Can help it. Editors is nien what knows every thing in the heaven above and the earth beneath. They is writers who doein't write any thing whatsoever. They is the biggest men you ever see. Managers is men as takes yn the tin and gives patent medicine "ads" tops c f columns next to retding matter, thirty-seven columns out of thirty-two. Proprietors an't any body. They an't ever seen. Printers' devils is the most important i persons n a nriuting office. They does the hardest work and gets the lent pay. Pressmen is—well, there wq,uldn't be no newspapers, no circus bills, without pressmen to i print 'em. Feeders s men what feeds on the fat of the , land. If I ever start a paper of my own I'll call it the Umbrella. Every body will take it. I heard the foreman tell this funny story to one of the "staff" the other day. It must have been funny, 'cause they both laughed. This- is the story:—" A gentleman was promenading the strEet with a littlls boy at his side, when the little fellow cried out: ' 0,1 pa, there goes an editor!' Hush, hush,' said the father, don't make sport of the poor man.:--God only knows what you may come to yet.' "—Albany Argus. -1 Mr. Jos. Young, of Golden Lyon Hotel, High-st.'; • Sunderland, Writes :--" I have suffered for many years with rheumatism ,brought on/by exposureand hard work at my trade, which is that of a shipbuilder. My suffer- ing was very great, and much of the time I was uMbre to work at all. I was never able to obtain Any per- manent relief until I used St. Jacobs Oil, and am proud to say that with using the Oil lam never troubled with the least pain. But more remarkable ,yet was the Case of my wife, who had nearly lost the use of her arm from rheumatism, but thank God and St. Jacobs Oil she has got all right again."

PAPERS FOR THE-PEOPEE.
B. HUGEL BETCE. PARTY WALL.

• The party wall is that boundary of the backyard which keeps your neighbour and yopself from embracing each other a You are fully aware 'that it is your wall, and your neighbour knows• that it is his, consequently you have a perfect right to put buckets and things on 'the top of the wall, and your neighbour has an equal right to push them off. Your neighbour has a legal right to drive a nail in thellop of the wall, and your hired girl ha l; the Lawful right to twist, tie, entangle, knot, ot other- wise fasten clothes lines to the aforesaid nail, in the manner heretofore set down and specified. If ,your neighbour takes a fancy to polish his nail as soon as ldur hired girl has put the clothes out to dry, he is Clearly. entitled to draw it out of the wall, and take it inside the house, leaving your clothes line- fastened upon space, or obeying the lay, of gravitation. Seeing that all this Isno clear, it is astonishing that the party wall should afford any grounds for contention:, yet such is the else sometimes. If yourncighbour 'and „yourself are on such friendly terms that your boys have friendly wrestling matches on the wall, and, whichever yard they f& into it doesn't cause a debate of course it doesn't matter. Bet suppose your neighbour has con- tracted the habit of sitting on the wall for a quiet smoke in the gloaming, and you give the surface a coat of tar as an ornamentation, he puts in a distinct claim for half of that wall, and tells you that you had no right to dcsit This is where the contention arises. If there is some- thing put on the wall that he cannot send off at one push, he talks An stage whispers about "some people's cheek," and uses many other phrases of a similar nature, which would lead one to think that tar is not sent' off a wall at one push. It you are a quiet, easy-going man, your neighbour will-build pigeon cotes.on the party wall, and then glare at ydu if you come out suddenly and frighten his birds. If you happen to be a man who wants Just his rights and no more, you will draw a chalk line exactly along .the middle of the wall, and your neighbour will imme- diately rub it out, and say that half of the line was upon his half of the wall. _ .

If you are an extremely stand-no-nonsense man, you will hire Anan to protect your half of that wall, and you will instruct him that he must not kill your neighbour's cat if he finds it sleeping on your half. When your neighbour and yourself have arranged .the walls in halves like this, there are some knotty legal points crop up with regard to the use of each hill. For instance, instead of driving the large nail for the clothes line into the top of the wall, suppose you drive it in the side. Your neighbour ascertains its exact positions, makes a hole opposite to it in his half, and nunchas your nail out, can you come upon him? Of course I know that you can come upon him with a ' club if you catch him at it, but what I mean is legally, for damages; be- cause if you can it would make the PAY. question very interesting if you sent an anonymous letter to your neighbour as a friend, putting him up to the dodge' and then arranged a Ist of old things on the line that you 'could prove were spoiled by the puncher. Assuming that you could make him pay for them, you could after- ward; make him a present of the things, thus easing your conscience, and punishing him at the same time; heaping coals of fire on his head, as it were. ' If you fix a sun-dial on the top of your half of the wall, and you find your neighbour stealing, the titne4 from it, I don't think you could claim damages from him, and the law won't exonerate you if yo il slap his face in the very act. Further, if you miss whole bundles of firewood, and the top of the wall under which it is kept is rubbed quite smooth, a jury wouldn't consider it, sufficient evidence that the wood had caused the smooth. ness alluded to in passing from your yard to your neigh- bour's, even if the neighbour's waistcoat buttons hart all the cloth worn off them. It you build your half of the wall ten feet hicher than his, and plant a Union Jack on the top to denote con- quest, the only satisfaction you have is to be sued for blocking up his light. I have sometimes wis,hed that our party wall had been left out 'altogether, so that Brown and myself might talk over the boundary question at close quarters, but as the march of civilisation has ordained it otherwise, and as Brown guar& his half with the vigilence of a Spartan, I have come to, the abrupt conclusion that the P.W. is a two-sectionali nuisance, affd although Brown's wife and mine spend the biggest part of every fine day leaning on it, and calling the other neighbours, I haven'tyet been perstleded into calling that & use woith mentioning. Over the Party Wall, • . You can't agree at all. Your neighbour and you with rage get blue, And threaten each other in court to sue, You swear you'll tight, but you never do, • , Over the Party Wall.
N.B.—This effusion will make the Editor sweat. I know it will, for be is dead nuts on "Rotes," but I really couldn't keep it. •

JIV"D BILLY'S PIG. BY Siam. When old Billy had finished his story of *buying a " cawve" there was some laughter, and he came in for a little banter, which he took in very good part. I had discovered by this time that Owd Billy ,was somewhat of a philosopher, and a rather noted character in the neighbourhood. One of his prominent charac- teristics was his amusingly quaint manner of telling a story. ,Every detail of the story of buying a dawve seemed, somehowto come out by accident; and he would quietly chuckle himself when he got to anything amusing, though it might be against himself. A young man who sat next Owd Billy, and wile) was known by the nickname of "Sorry," said, " Wey, yo' hedn'd much off, Billy, to give *a hofe of a eawve up to be wasted because somebry sed as id hed inflamma- tion." -" Wey, wod wod teaw a done if tha'd a bin i' my place, Sorry ?" asked Owd Billy. " Awd a hetten id." $ : " Wod, thiser "Aye, awd a tried." Aye, un tha'd a lookt wee!, wodn'd ta, walkin' nbeawt t' streets wi' thi belly Dill o' inflammation." "Inflammation be hanged! ,Awd a risked id." • q Ateve no deawt tha wod, Srry. Aw'm 'certain as heyt owt if Um werahunpy., Slit aw'm nod thad *ay. Aw want to'bisatistied as amyt's gradely afoor avatouch id." • • "Aar dorn'd think as yo' were so varra particular when yo' geet thad Guinea pig killed un ate id." "Aw dudn'd heyt id o', Sorry." "Well, but yo' ate some on id." "Aw dud, certain." - "Well, aw shouldn'd like to face owt o' thad sooart," said Sorry. I said to Owd Billy, How did you come to have a Guinea pig killed, Billy ?" "Well, if aw mon tell yo' t' truth, mesther, id were moor a lark then owt," said he. I said," Well, I never heard tell of a Guinea pig being killed tjefore. Let's hear how- it came about?' "Gooa on, tell him t' tale, Billy. Yo' mut as weel as nod," said a red-faced, round-paunched man on my left, and he laughed and shook his corporation as if recalling something amusing in the story. "Well, yo' known," said Owd Billy, Commencing, "aw'd bowt this Guinea pig thinkin' as id wod be a nice plaything, un summat as wom'd as common as hanaries, in dogs, un cats, un wod nod, un aw thowt id would pleeas eawr fooak. Un id dud for a bit, yo' lthow. Id were a varra cleyn lookin:thing, yo' know, Cm o' thad, but it could.noather sing nor bark nor nowt. un we soon geet tired on id. Aw darsay aw'd hed id summat like five or six week when aw thowt as aw'd hey a bit ofat lark wi' id. "At t' time.as aw'm talkin' abealvt we bed a mon as used to gooa o reawnd, t' nebberhood kiln' pigs.; Id were hill job, yo' know. Un he thowt summat of hisser, aw con tell yo'. He used to brag as he could kill a pig sherper nor owt for miles reawnd. But, heaweyer, to ged on wi' ml tale, aw thowt aw'd see wod he could do t' pig-Irillin' line. tfe'd never killed a pig far me afoor, sooa aw thowt aw'd give him a job. Aw sent a lad db,wn, to 1174 him wheal he could come un kill me a pig. He sent:whrd sailed come t'Thursdaymornin'followin', un as aw mist be ready for him, un hey plenty o' hot watther ready bi ten o'clock o' t' mornin'. Well, of coourse, e.sesent him word as aw'd be ready for him. Neaw, at thad‘ime aw hed a pigcoyt at back o' th' heawse. sooa o' t' Thursday mornin as he hed to come aw o ready for him. Aw geet a lot o' boilin' watther ready. Well, at ony rate, aw filled t' boiler, un aw put a big posnet full o' watther on t' fire. Un aw putt' guinea pig t' pigcoyt at back o' th' heawse, yo' knot Aw thowt there should be no disappointment through me, dun yo' see? " Abeawt a-quarter to ten his lordship coom lorryin' up t' back wi' another chap, un they were carryin' his stock between urn. He bed his steel up his knife wi', him' un he'd his brat on, un o appo-pie order. Aw lest him in at back dooar, un he sed, 'Neaw. Bill, heaw are yo' for watther?' Aw showed him t' boiier un t' posnet, un he sed, Thad'll do.' Then we went to t' ack, un he seet his stock un geet o ready, un sed. Nea.w,then, wheer's this pig?' "Aw sed, It's i' t' coyt.' " Ha sed,' Aw dorntikee id,Bill.' " Abbut it's theer,' aw sed. "He hed another look,un then be sed,'Aw'll be hanged if aw con see ony pig here.' "w sed, Look reawnd t' corners, un the!' find id. Id isn'd such a big un.' ' "He went inside o' t' coyt, un id seems he see summat stor. He med a grab at id, but id slipt past him. But, heawever, he med another grab. un catched id, un he browt id eawtside i' one hand, un he sed, This is o as aw con find i' t' coyt, Bill. Wod's ta ce' id ?" "Aw sed, That's id.' ," Thad's wod id. Wad's ta.meean ?' "Aw sed, That'S t' pig.' "Eh, dear o' me! heavr he dud coss. He sed he worn'd hewn to be med a foo' on. Aw should hey to pay him whether there were a pig to kill or nod. "Aw sed, 'ma's come to kill a pig. hesn'd ta?' "He said, eye.' * • "Ave sed, Well, thad's a pig; ged id killed, un than} ,ged paid.' "Well, after a good deeal o' ado, he browt id to t' stock. un he howded id wi' one hand whet he stuck t' knife into i 1 wi' t'tother. Aw tiled him gooa abeawt his werk gradelv, un he scodened id, un scraped id, uri' hung id up ith' heawse, just like any other pig. Aw towd him to dome.t' day after un cut id up un then aw'd pay him. He coom un cut id up, un then aw paid him eighteenpence for his job. "-But he never heerd t' last o' thad job; for after id geet eawt everybody were on to him abeawt id. "Well, after he'd cut id up aw put id i' sawt, un then aw hung th' hams up i'th' heavrse, after they were cured. Aw reckoned o t' lot to ke woth abeawt th' eighteen- pence as aw'd paid for t' killin' on id." .1 said; "What did you do with it after you had cured it? Did you eat it?" "Well, some on id. Ave swapped one o'h' hams ?" "What did you swap one of the hams for ?" I askedi " Aw'll tell yo'. Aw happened to gfta deawn to Joe Hartley's, t' cobbler's, one day, for a pair o' shoon as aw'd sent to be soyled, un whel aw were timer he sed, Doesn'd ta want a new pair o' shoon, Bill?' "Ave sed, !Nay, nod just at present. Brass is nooan ao plentiful, or else ge darsay aw could do wi' a pair.' "Well, we talked a bit, un at last aw bethowt misel as a mit as Weel swap one o' ml hams, sooa a sed, 'By guy aw'll tell ths wrid aNy'll do. Aveve a ham i yonder at Imam; if tha'll mek me a pair o' new Voots that's hey Li for um.' 'He sed; 'Wad sooart a' one is id 2" "Avesed, It's a hooam's-cured un. It's bin curd abeawt three months.' "It's nod bin spoiled i' t' curia', aw suppooase?' he sed. " • "Ave sed, It's as weel cured as id con be.' Varra weel, aw'll mek tha a pair for id.' • " Well, he mezzered ma, un he med ma a rale good pair e shoon, un when he'd med urn he sent urn up wi' a lad, un aw sent th' ham deawn wi' t' same lad. . "There wete a bonny to do, aw con tell yo'. flecoom up to eawr heawse wi' th' ham, un he duct kick up a shindy. Aw talked abeawt fooaktnekkin' bergains un stickin' to um, bud id med no difference. sHe threw th' ham at mo un walked eawt o'th' heawse. swearin' as he'd put moit' cooart for t' brass. Aw hed o' t' teav laughin' at him.

, Mn: Jo- MORLEY IN' LANCASHIRE.—Mr. John Morley %visited Darwen on ,Wednesday and opened a Liberal, 'l3ailar. Addressing the company, he spoke of the im- portance of an amendment of the law of registration. He also pointed out that in 1835 Mr. Chambierlain deplored that the reform of Dublin Castle would form the work of the new Parliament, and that in 1883 Lord Hartington made ' a remarkable announcement in Lancashire as to compensation to the licensed victuallers. Addressing a .great Liberal meeting at Blackburn, in the evening, Mr. Jahn Morley acknowledged an-address presented to him by the Irishmen of the town, which, he obsnrved, was couched in the most moderate language. Thii he regar- del as a sign that the Irish question had entered on a phase which the most sanguine could not have expected t*enty years ago. That the : question %should have so advanced was due to courage, foresight, and unselfish sacrifice of the leader of the Liberal party. Of all Mr. Gfadstone's achievements for his country, mime would be thought sci Feat, so glOijous, so consoling as the work done tor justice and humanity in reconpiling the English and Irish peoples. Irish nationality had been wrlded together by the tradition of fcdmmon oppression and wrong, as it was now by 'a com- mon hope. Lord Randolph Churchill had spoken of this as a golden Parliamentary age, but to him "(Mr. gorley) it was odious, and not at all a sign of a golden age, to aft see Irish members 1 kell up and their steps dogged by detectives. Mr. B .wls/uld to ,get rid Of the new. feeling of responsibi ty anicing Irish Members and the Irish people, to destroy the , growing goodwill between them and outselves, and throw us back into the old sullen fureace of distrust, .suspicion, and mutual lhate. Adverting to crime in.lreland, Mr Morley aiclitfiat coer- cion had failed to calm agrarian troubled. The Govern- said they would be willing to • extend local self- government to Ireland when there was loyalty to the Crown and Constitution'; but their action, he contended, was hot calculated to induce those feelings of loyalty and attacbanent to the Constitution which were so much de- sired. The, Chief Secretary treated the Irish Members, with the easy contempt of white men for the negroes of athe cotton, plantation. : Thfif anticS"and drolleries itmused him, add if ttliiy carried it too far he knew he could always lock them up. But he (Mr. Morley) be- hoved that the' dark hour for Ireland had passed, and that she had found friends encl comforters who would never desert her.

ALLEGED 7RIZE TIGHT AT ORFORD. • At the County Petty Sessions, t Warrington, on Wednesday morning, two forge labourers, named James Reid, of Ca,rlisle-st., and John Troy, of 8, hiferry's-yard;, appeared to answer summonses charging them with having committed a breach of the peace, by fighting together. at Orford, on tint 15th inst. Constable Monogban, of the borough police force, was the principal witness. He deposed td hearing, on the day, in question, that there was a prize fight going on near Orford Schools, and said that he saw a crowd of shoat. ,300 people there. Troy, who was bleeding. was coming away .with a black and Swollen eye. There was considerable disorder. In answer to Mr. Marson, who presided on the Bench, witness said that he understood that the tight was for money, but this 'Was denied by the defendants. Another witn-ss, , al lad named Isaac Smith, said that the two,.defen-, dents had their coats and waistcoats off, and that one of them had his shirt off. The magistrates ordered defendants to be bound over to-be of good behaviour, themselves in kld each, ? and•two g-dre- ties of £5 each, or, in default,lourtezin clays' impri- sonment.

A Meeting of the ccmmittee of the Warrington Temperance Federation was held at the Horse= market-street Coffee Tavern, on Tuesday evening, when it was resolved to forward to the liouse of Commons a petition in rhe following terms : "To the honourable the Commons of the United ling- done in Parliament as,serpbled.—The humble petition of the Warrington Temperance Federation Sheweth:—That your petitioners have heard with regret and Oran of the proposition which has been submitted to your honour- able House forijhe taxation of the people in order tO Par: off those dealers in intoxicating liquors who may here- after not succeed in maintaining* their licentes for the sale of such liquors. That your petitioners are con- vinted that the trade carried on under sanction of these licenses, whilh enriching the._ tradrrs; lmm been a most serious obstacld to national prosperity and morality. That these licenses have been issued by irreSponsible authorities; frequently regardless of the demands or .wishes of the communities amongst whom they. have been granted. That .7.-gur petitioners have grievously suffered from the large expenditure rentereeneeessary ly the existence of these drink shops, arid strongly ob- ject to having a fresh burden imposed on the industry,of 'he country m order to provide pensions for thilse whose licensesmay not be renewed. That your petitioneTs are of opinion that the VocaltGovernment Bill, clause 12, sec- tion 7, should be amended so as to provide right of ap- peal.in all cases where the decision of the ideal justices disallows a report 'against -the renewal of a license. Wherefore your petitioners humbly pray,that your hon- ourable House will be pleased to reject the Compensation Clauses of the Local Giverninent Bill. An your peti- tioners, as in duty bound, will ever pray, &e." The peti- tion, which was forwarded on Thursday. wars- signed by the following members and officials of the Federation : Revs. S. Wilkinson (president), John Yonge, G. Allton, J. Warnock, E. Moore, W. Graham, JosepliP Flanaghan, J. J. Longhorn, iec. • Messrs. .E. Twiss, Hy., Roberts, John Walker James 'Dodds, Robert Garnett (J.P.), J. H. Gornall (LP:), D. Houghton (assistant sec.), W. Roberts ' (treasurer), R. Roberts, and R. Storey.

A concert that was well attended was held on Thursday evening, at Padgate School, in connection with the Padgate and Orford Habitation (2,025) of the Primrose League. Prigs: to it, the annual busi- ness meeting of the Habitati*n, was held in an ad- joining class-room, presided over by Mr! William Ap- pleton, at which the following elections were made —ruling councillor, Mr. George Comber, Middleton Hall; secretary, Mr. F. Appleton; and treasurer, Mr. G. Mather. The ENecntive Council was re- appointed, the names of Miss Witter andlllfiss pleton being.added to thelist. There was a numer- ous attendance at the concert, at the commencement of which Mr. William Appleton presented the ruling coun- cillor, Mr. Comber, with a badge of office, subscribed for by the dames and knights of the Habitation. -After- wards an address WaS, delivered by Mr. T. W. Legli, M.P. for the 4ewton Division, who referred to the pleasure tat' he felt to ' find a branch of the Primrose League had been' established in that neighbourhood. The fact of the Primrose League being in existence was an evider.ce in itself of the healthy state of the Conservative party. The Habitation had been but a short time in existence, tut he did not doubt that they were all familiars with the objects for which the Priiprose League was inaugurated.l The league was in the Ant place started to commemo- rate the career'of the late Lord Beaconsfield, and it was one of the Mat means of uniting, in :one common band those chases who were in favour of maintaining the in- stitutions of whicli they were all so prowl, and which hail been handed down to them by their forefathers. The league started in a wall .waii. The numbers were ridiculously small when the league was inaugurated, but now it had attained the dimensions of 700,000 members. He need hardly, point out, that, so manyloeople, pledged Ito support ConservatiVePiinciples formal 'no mconsider- able body in the British electorate, and - the influence a .80 large and important a body had been manifested on. 'several occasions, and notably during the last general I election. There were two reasons for the success of roe Primrose League:. One of them was' to be und in that union of the various classes wbieh their , opponents had always maintained to ê finpossible, and the second was due, he thought, to the inclusion of the female set. lsro institution had so provoked tlie gibes and sneers- of their ofiponents, as had the Primrose League: The Liberals had exhausted the vocabularies of 'heir wrath upon the subject, but that was perhaps a greater proof than any of the value of the League., Their opponents had, all the same, endeavoured to imitate the League, for they had. endeavoured to establish leagues of their own. It had been proposed to establish' an League," and a "Red' .Rose Ivague," and various at-. tempts had been made, he believed, in this direction; even "Sweet William, had been suggested as the name of a future Liberal League. Bus all these attempts had 'ended in disastrous failure; He was inclined not to 'speak with too much confidence in regard to the impor- tant question—would the League last? Everything ume to an end, aqg they should not be too confident as to HIT permanency of the Prim- rose League. But without looking to the future, ft would perhaps be sufficient if they considerid the past history of the League. 'He thought that there was no one in that room who would deny that the Primrose Leue' had achieved great things in the past, and that were it to cease to-morrow its effect would be per- manently elt in British politics. It was haidlyntdessary for him to recommend to their favourable consideration ,the course of policy that had been pursued by the Con- servative Government. Perhaps it would 'be Sufficient to compare it in a; few words with the Government formed by Mr: Gladstone in 1880. In a yeavr two the country wa broiled in utterly purposelessMnd useless wars; anarchy was found to be existing in Ireland, and disaffection atlipme, and there was a general confusion I of things altogether. They found also that the national expenditure had increased to prodigious limits. _The Unionist Government had now been in office abourtNfo rfars, arid he took upon himself to Say that not for a long time had the position of this country been so good as regarded .foreign affairs as it was at the present time. This was owing to the statesmanship of their illustrious leader—Lord Salisbury. It would be admitted by most of those present tbat a certain revival of.trade and confidence had sprung up sincgthe-exist- ence of the present Government. He would also point to. the 14aCt that for the first time for some years this Union.: ist Government had found itself in possession,nf-a surplus of two millions, and had been able to take a penny off the income tax. It, seethed to him that these were no inconsiderable triumphs. Having also upheld the policy of the Government in regard tit Irish affairs, Mr. Legn -aid he could not hop thinking thatWhed the country again came to vote on the eternal frish question the voice of common sense would again assert itself. He looked forward with some confidence to the result of the next appeal, whenever it might come, for be was certain that the people would again vote for tir men who had honestly maintained-theirAconvictions, and would sup- port to the utmost of :their power the . integrity, of the empire to which'. 'they were all so proud to belong, (Cheers.)—A musical .prpgramtne was afterwards,' gone .through, and the meetig concluded with the Usual votes pf thanks. ' _ - .

Birchall, gave an Interesting address on the condi/don and prospects of the sociaty,/in which he referred to the correspondence which lately took ,p‘aee through the columns of "The ExarAiner" on the subject of Co-operation In Warrington: '

div.head: • TEE RESULTS OF 'CRITICISM
div.p: • TEE RESULTS OF 'CRITICISM

ButcuALL said : I have latelY spent considerable time . and trouble in reviewing the coixlition and pros- pects of our society. It is pleasing to see that its steady progress is still tmcheiked, a list of nearly 200 new meth- bers being presented to-night for our approval. Yeti during the past quarter we have been subjected to severe public criticism; the result being, as usual, to popularise the society, and to increase•the number of applicants for membership. Seeing then that it has become an important institution—its 2,000 members ,cotriprising with their families probably a seventh of tile population ot Warrington-4 will not be out of place if I take this opportunity of reviewing our posi- tipn in its relations to the various sections of the com- mtwity of which we form so large a part, to re-state the principles on which it is based, and the motives wbich first led to its creation, and the important objects in view, which give a valid reason for its existence.

is now al;Ot-it -2.-8-ier-s-aio—sie-c-e a few earnest arti- saps, anxious to improve thehliwn conditions and that of their fellows, rnet in an upper room in Orford-st., and, after much deliberation and review of their small pecuniarrresources, decided to inaugurate the Warring- ton Equitable Industrial Co-operative Society. That one material consideration in their scheme' wds that it wailed add somewhat to thqir scanty incomes there is no doubt. But that there was also prescht to the minds of a num- ber of them, visions of still greater good to be realified I can bear heartfelt witness ; visions of a time when 'men should have becomo wiser, stronger, and more self- reliant—quicker •to perceivethe vast advantages which intelligent co-operation with their fel4;iws would give, aqd when after a training in this, the simplest form of cfoperatiOn, they should learn, at length, how the com- bined small savings of the many in the hands of the wise and trusted leaders could belnade as mighty in the production of wealth and social comfort for the many, As the riches of the millionaire, too often used for his own iriersonal aggrandisement. •

div.head: -THE ERINCTFLKS OF THE SOCIETY.
div.p: -THE ERINCTFLKS OF THE SOCIETY.

The men who thus met ill the autumn of 1860, several of whom still take&ctive part in our management, were dtikermined that it Mould be based on fixed and definite' principles. From those principles lam proud to say th'at it has never swerved i I will tell /on In a few \Words what some of ,those principles are. Add I especially commend what lam bout to say to the attention , of those df our members who have not long been connected with us, and who may not have considered thoitghtfully the grounds upon which our association is based.. First. then, they determined to Set an example of honeit and Upright dealing.. That sok far as they knew„ no Spurious or adulterated goods should be sold by them to impose up.on their customers, that all articles so far as possible should yield a, fair profit, knowing that no dealer can sill at or below cost price without loss requiring to be aade up in somvither way • that no 'fdelings of rivalry 'should be entertained towards individual or neighbour-'in,g tradesmen ; that selling prices should be regulated by those of the ordinary.rum of respectable traders, whose actien is in harmony with foregoing principles; that no attempt should be made in any way to tine)er-sell them, but that the well-known'and mischievous custom of" ctitting"—that is of selling certaifi articles at or below cost Price in (order 'to attract buyers—should on no account be practised in their establish- ment. Seeing what a terrible curse the credit system had been, they decided that it should tip rigidly excluded from their operation and that cash payments should be their invariableaule. And, further, that the employes of the society should have a weekly half-holiday; and that all profits, after providing sub- stantial reserves and paying 5 per cent, on capital should be divided in proportiv to purchases amongst all its memlOrs. • That the adoption and energetic practicei of these and similar principles, has from time to timj drawn down upon us criticisms and comments, fair and othervMse, is not Up be wondered at. That has alwayS been the lot of the pioneers in any .department of prac- tical reform. I3ut we have long passed • the period of doubt and discouragement, and 'glancing back upon what we have already accomplished, we may look with satisfaction to the spread of our principles and to the increasing number of participators in the advantages resulting. therefrom. . THE PRESENT POSITION AND CONSTITIITIOk OF THE

div.head: SOCIETY.
div.p: SOCIETY.

Our society now oCcupies'a position of 'which its mem- bers may well be-proud. Its constitution' is thoroughly democratic, every member having equal 'rights in its government, whether his invested capital be large or small. Its course of action is pre-eminently unselfish, offering tb the applicant for membership to-day, equal . terms with its 'oldest mtmbers,,,a, full share of the ac- cumulated advantages gained d ,uring 28 yea*. It ,has all the-Advantages of a savings Bank to its members but with double rate interest, yet it enables them to save without pinching themselves. It is in full sympathy with every movement wherever it may have been origin- ated, which has for its aim and opject the physical, men- tal, or moral eleVation of the 'people. ' That it has been very successful as a commercial undertaking is beyond aillitVil. It is not only paying s'per cent, on its capital, ' biitrit is Also distributing as dividend in purchases over £7,000 per annum. In a word, ',that conditions could be , more favourable to surtess than that of a business con- cern with ample capital contributed by some 2,000 mem- ers; all of whom are buyers from it for cash only, thns4 making their own irivtment proddctive and also pro.. viding a Constant supply of customers .without the rialt of a single bad debt. And this is our happy positiv "- day. . i

div.head: PHOGRESS or CO-OPEAATTON
div.p: THE PHOGRESS or CO-OPEAATTON

Co-operation has indeed worked wonders lit thilGUfl try during the comparatively few years of it existence. .It has united in its great sphere of usefulness, rinn of every shade of rgligio'us and political creed, and has en- rolled amongst its honoured leaders me* of the most divergent opinions on other subjects. It has drawn out tiid dgmonstrated the capacity of workingmen or the organisation and satisfactory nianagement of Mtge in- dustrial ad commercial undeirtakings, as witness the hundreds of successful co-operative apcieties and, notably, the great Manchester Wholesale, With its enor-, mous turnover of £7,000,000 per annum—one of 'the greatest commercial enterprises the world h -yet seeh. . And this was originated and brought to its present' cori- dition by. British workmen, ;

- ITS let7lytill. That we are very far trona realising the full tattle .of CO-operation as a powerfuldgent for the amelioration of st al conditions ang for helping in the solution of the ~di culties between eapital and labour is plain tp every earnest student of this subject. a For capital and labour may fight till one or the other of the combatants 4s ex- hausted. and the victor will have suffered terrible loss. But it can oily be when the co-operative principle (it may be in some form not yet developed) is brought to bear, recognising the true relative value of each and their mutual dependence on each other; then a great step iet advance will have been made towards that grand era of peace dn earth and goodwill' amongst men, for which men have- so long hoped and prayed. We are glad to think that our society is ene branch of this great and beneficent movement, and that while yielding sub- stantial results to its members it is also one of those 'educative influences which are silently preparing the way for that glad time when capital and labour shall no longer be arrayed in hostility to each other, but being cordially united shall work together for the universal well-being and happiness of mankind. The address was very attentively listened to by the large number present at the meeting, and its close there Was tOrdial, applause. It was also suggested that ,it should be printed 'and-ptiblicly distributed.

Three commercial travellers sat over their wine and cigars one day after dinner, •in a comfortable inn in Devonshire. They Yiere "jolly good fellows," knowing each other as Tom. Diek, and Harry. After comparing notes on.the state of trade, etc., jokes and stories went around. till, at last, Tom and Dick began chaffing Harry on th.e shabby condition of. his head, for his hair was fast failingout, and the sparse quantity he still retained was quite gray, and both de- clared he had deceived them concerning his age, for his scanty gray hairs proved that he bad already "fallen into the see I the yellow leaf?' Dick deektred that, he knew of a sure remedy. Harry innocently and' anxiously inquired what it was. Dick told him: "Cut half a dozen red onions into thick slices; rub your head thoroughly with them, and—leaving the slices on Tour head—sit in the 114 sun for three hours "Nonsense I" Marry objected. "Well, if you don't choose to tir it, go bald!" Harry secretly resolveil to try it, and did. The next day his mischievous fiends spied him sitting in the sun, in the stable yard, hfil Ifead.plastered With onions, hfp'eyes full el their juice, and streaming with tears. CHAPTER XW.

STRICKEN. _,41 Her apron thrown over her head-,-for the night, though it was July, was damp and chill=---Phyllis followed Tom Chilton to the Three Griffins. Shedid not even call out to her mother,who she hoped was -asleep, .but Jail the door, on the latch and went at once with Tom without asking a single question. She felt as if she ,were almost afraid to . speak, and. therefore trusted to what he Would tell her. He, how- ever, vouchsafed no remark till they neared the Three Griffins; then* he said; "He's very bad, Phyllis, but you're no voward,• you'll know-how' to fitee it "}ace what r., asked Phyllis, after, A second or two, !luring which ,she was contending with a rising lump in her throat. "Death, I'm afraid. He's had a sort of fit," "Good Heavens We ought to have brought mother." ' "Best get him home if we can, and,not scare her before he's in his own house.'! Through the bar of the Three Griffins, 'Tom Chilton led Phyllis. It -was the first time she bad been there, having been brought up by her, mother with a holy dread of taverbs7 and 'she, shuddered visibly as she passed through and ialialeirthe strong mixed odour of spits and tobacco. The bar was Very crowded, -and. every eye was turned on Phyllis, ivliose rare beauty startled not a little more than 'one Of these' assembled thtre.' • An awc,':however, ford tunately for her, , had fallen on the usually noisy habitues of the place, arid they contented themselves with looking at mstead of spea.kiag to her, ,In aninner porn' On a black "horsehair Sofa,lar Slnion Knight. The landlady of the Three Griffins, a lnixotaxlarne,in a flowery big-patterned dr,ess with flaunting ribbons; was leaning over himbathing„ his head. , lie seemed , quite unconscious, and did not even recognise PhYlliS when. she approached him, though his eyes were wide open; but his face was redder, .than Phyllis ever reingrabered to have seen it • before, .and his loud steatoiciaa breathing quite frightened her. • She knelt -down beside him and kissed his, rough 'hand, but he did not heed her ; then she turned ap- ,,pealinglY to Toth 'Chilten,as though askinrhim what she should do.. The stifling atmosphere of the place. I- well-nigh choked her,for the fumes from the tap-room' penetrated even there, and not a Symptom was there of an, open window. • "The doeto?Will be here directly. I thought he would have been here now," said Chilton.' "lie will tell us what to do." •At this moment the local practitioner tame in, a smile on hit benign countenance, a smile which, how- ever, speedily changed into a very grave expression when he 'saw Simon Knight.' . The first thing he did wasi to throw open the window, and 'then without asking even a single question he proceeded to bleed the patient. "Can't we take him home, away from this dreadful place ?" incautiously pkaded Phyllis., . "Dreadful place, indeed 1" Tom retorted the bux landlady; who, notwithstanding her gay exterior,was a bit of a shrew. ' Dreadfutplace, indeed! Who are you I should like to know.. A bit cl a hussy like yon that you,should Call my house a dreadful place." , Ilhe doctor laid hand on her arm. "My dear madam,pray leave wrangling alone till this poor maif is better, oe--" He did not finish this portion of his sentente, bat turning to Phyllis, said— "The bleeding .successful, I-hope We' May be able to take pint, father home in a few tours." ;And then for some moments there was a deep silence in thalittle room, • • A few drops of dark purple blood came from the arm of the unconscious man, but it did not flow freely. The little' that came seemed momentarily, at all events, to relieve his head, for, he heaved a sigh and muttered some indistinct words which no one could. comprehend unless-it were Tom Ohilien,who,standing near his head, leaned his ear doWn to his lips in order to catch the meaning of the thick guttural sounds. some request 'probablyr about the settlement of hiS affairs for his Child or his wife, for Tom Chilton asked the doctor in somewhat excited ac- cents— " If you cannot give this man life, at least can you not free the brain from pressure for a few minutes so as to enableldm to speak, reveal something he has on his inhidi" doctor shook his head. "The one is as diffi- cult as the other," he said "the brain freed for a short time, he would probably recover." . • " Ah, it is a pity, a 'sad, sad , pity," muttered ,Chilton, rusif he were more taken up by the wish to hear somethin,g further On the subject about which he had fancied, he had te'some alrittering' than with the desire to restore his' old friend to his family and his business. Meanwhile . Simon ' Knight had relapsed into a state of stupor that might have been death itself, but for Iliethard I btatithingand. the flushed face. 'lt:was very evident to all those who stood by that :the end was not far Off, rind that the doctor's help was of little While they Stood watching there,

.: . , agaii. pleading that he might be taken horrie, a loud shrill crY startled them. It proceeded from the tap-room divided only from the parlour. by a glass do 4 Beiore any one had time to go forward and inquire into its cause,' a woman, wrapped in a long eycloak,rushe,d frantically in and threw herself on r ' knees at - the: foot of the sofa. It was Hannah . .f . night. Weary of lying awake waiting for Simon to come, she :had got up intending to console' herself by i d few words with Phyllis, but found the girl had gore and , the front door, open. , With a sort of in- stiAct she had rolled herself in a waterproof, and, barefooted, had made for the, Wove griffins, ..ljtOe expecting, liOvever, Such 4 scene as , . that whicli presented Itself. ' Querulously drunk ?Sion Knight so' frequently was that she always , dreaded lest . sooner or later there would be a ! terrible- encounter with .some man in a like comp- ' lion ; but that he should be lying there gasping be- i*een life and death was such 'a' shock, to his dutiful, though hardly-tried, wife, that she fainted and for a time looked even more like death than t man *hose end seemed to be fast approaching. •P, 1 ,14, Sills:. temperament was scarcely a` calm one, yet she ,pOsseSsed .the courage an& determination which. keeps feelingain control when danger is imminent.‘ She raised. her, Mother, and almost carrying her 'fo the open wind*, bathed her , face with ; sOme ' €old water which was standing by, .and in terms of the ,gentlest endearment, caressed her back to a.' knowledge of what' WaS sing on around her. Alas, ' the knowledge was no enviable one, for scarcely had Mrs. .Knight recovered, from her . tem- porary prosttntion, than the gurgling in Simon 's throat 'having . ' considerably increased, suddenly stoppekaltogether, and 'there was a dead cairn, for each one of those whil were gathered together in that little room knew that he was standing in' the prow eence of death. Death in one of its most 'end moods, 441 came amongst them, not with a kimffy hand con- 'difeting a righteous man to his rest, but snatching up; A sinner at the. very zenith of his vicious . plea- sure, and making the bystanders tremble as they thought of tie wrath to come. • Yes! the imperious husband and severe father had put down his 'burden of earthly care, and Phyllis and her mother, as the Stood clinging. id each other ' beside the gradually coldening corpse,:- already won-. tlered what life Would be like without this strong +ll And hand to sway them. Was Toth' Chilton going to take the,place that had been just vacated? For -he lett ,them both away upstairs into the landlady's' room till such time as some warmer clothing could be provided for Mrs. Knight, or .a' conveyance of . some sort be found to take her home. Phyllis was -thankful to Tom Chilton for his kindly 'care of them 'both. She was too crushed and. Woe-skirl:en te be -otherwise than grateful to 41:nyone Who 'Was ready to help her in Ihislout of trial; still 'as she reinem, 1 bored that last conversation she „had had with her father only rt:few hours pratzions, and how he in- sisted that Tom Chilton shdrild be linked with all the actions of her future life, she almost shuddered while she thanked him. ` HOW 'much' had he had tu do with what had just taken place she wondered,; in what way had he been: 'mixed 'up with that interview with Mr: Stanhope' which for all she •Inew,,. had brought .about this terrible result ? ' She was longing to ask him, but could not till she had got her niother, who seemed almost stUpified by the shock, safe back to ,the brick house and toled. ! , Before this had been accomplished, and Toni had erformed some Of ' the sad details necesAary at the Three Griffins, it was already daylighi, and then he 'too, wended IN way to the brick houSe to ask Phyllis for a, "bit of breakfast,'" as he said. , He was quite right in suPpOlsirig that she would not , have gone to bed.; • . She had lighted.. the .kitchen' ,-fge, and was trying to make the kettle boil, in order ,to give :her :mother a cup Of ::tea; probably sh& ex:' pected Torn; or was it old habit? bet-she had set three cups and saucers on the table. , Toni looked very, white and, weary when he entered; even men of Tom Chilton's vagrant habits and hardiness of frame' do not go through scenes like
t P

the one he had just witnessed without their nerves .1 being tried and their pulses quickened. In fact, to a casual observer, it would almost have Seemed as if I that night's work had shaken him even more than • it had skaken Phyllis; for, with her, the dazed sense- • don of the first shock: lied hot yet passed; and a looked unnaturally composed. She had not siled one single tear; they were all to be shed in copious floods when the full knowledge of What had happened/I mid what the future had in store should come upori •,'; her. ••\ Tom Chdton had entered through the yard where the men were already astir, but scareely working, for • ,they were too much awed by the news that had ' degicended on them like a thunderclap. Phyllis held out her hand when she saw Tom, and said, I thank you," in a cold,measured voice, which had so • much • • strangeness. in it; that it made him very sad. "lon have nothing to thank me for, Phyllb; ; I have only done what I should have done for any man under Similar circumstances." " I should like to know how it all happened, if you do not mind telling me, Tom,"• she said quietly, looking into the fire instead of into his face while she spoke. - " Well, your father went into town yesterday, it seems. Do you know whit for, Phyllis ? "To see Mr. Stanhope, I believe, ' Mie answered. in- ) a•very low voice. • ' • ' "Was there any cause, for a dispute between your father and-Mr. Stanhope;do you know ?" Phyllis did not speak for a minute or two, then her answer was a question; "Did they have a dispute ?" "Something very like it, ram afraid. Can-yot gueis.what it was about ?" • • "How should I, Tom ?" she replied just , a trifle tartly; t` besides I should like to know how, in wonder's name, you were mixed up with it." "Don't miStake,'tss, I have naught to di, with it. I had been to Stanhope's, having a bit of talk with - Aunt Purvis on a little matter of business. Our Talk . over, I walked straight along the equare towards the Victoria Station, when who should I see standing at the corner of the street leading to the Station but your father..'` Come on, Tom, my boy, and have a drink;' he called out cheerily; but I shook my head, for I saw at once that he had ,had more than was ,( good for him. He insisted, however ; you know what 'he was when the drink was in him." „

Phyllis sighech , " lje led the way into a neighbouring public-house, and was resolved to Stand treat." •, ) •. • , I "Oh, Tom, hovreould you let him." • 'k • • "I could not help it; on my soul, Phyllis, t could • not. You. . know how positive he was,, Besides, . how was Ito guess what was going to happen? Well, I. we had a drink; I very little, for yell know I am not, • a drinking man ; and .then I tried ,to persuade him to come along with me home to Wandsworth. lie contented. after a while, and I got him out of the pub. along on to railway ,platfortn, he declaiming 7 • all the tithe, till I thought we should have a crowd and the police. .. I can't rightly tell you; what it was 4 all about, but I gathered that .he had been to Stan- hope's and had a blazing row with the master." . • Phyllis looked very white, but though Tom stopped she did not attempt toCrosk-examine Win. -110 went on after a second or two by asking= , " Was your father ever mixed up with, the Stan- hopes in old years, before he married your mother V' ' r ' Ido not know," answered Phyllis; ".I-think la knew them or- he would net have beeii lying near Warleigh and have' got acquiihted Ivith . mother. Somehow I think Mr. Stanhope - helped I' father to-get into business,, but father never liked it is to be.mentioneil, and lias abused Mr. :Stanhope - awfully of late." . "Of course he knew them; why he was courting aunt Purvis, but whether he and Stanhope , wasn't ' mixed up in some dirty transaction is what I'm sus- pecting." • - " Lor, fancy Mr. Stanhope in a dirty transaction I " -Torn Chilton smiled as he noted that ,it was not about her father, but about Mr. -Stanhope that she expressed surprise. He said nothing, however, and it was evident that Toni' Chilton knew far more than he intended to say. He only muttered half to him- self, "1 wonder what that row was about !" He saw from the expression on Phyllis's face that he had guessed rightly when he imagined she was concerned in it; but though he was made unhappy by her philanderings, with Geoffrey, he was too manly to tvit her under existing circumstances, so he let the subject drop, and -very Bonn Phyllis went Upstairs with her mothar's tea, and Tom was left for a while to chew the end of his meditations in the kitchen. Aye, and chew it well too, for Mrs. Knight had such a fit of sobbing that it was sonic time before Phyllis could leave ter. , , The outcome of his thoughts lie decided did nr amount to much, and yet he felt sure there was a gook, deal of mystery lurking about, if only he could gather it up and make something substantial of it. ,The two or three words he ,believed Simon Knight to have muttered gave him some sort of a clue; still; he was not quite 'sure enough that they had been spoken at ' all, for him to feel justified in acting on them. . When Phyllis rothrned into the kitchen Torn was still-absorbed in-his ruminations. 'She, too, kad silo listened mi„,•ll.t have heard a muttering that would have astonished her. A ring at tli, outer door, how- ' ever, prevented any conversation between thorn; and I Torn; shaking off his meditative mood, went to answer the summons. . (To bc. continued. )

LILLE, SIIIMAY Num-Lt.—The returns of the election Ire now complete with the.exception of one commune. rhe total numbAr of \registered electors in the depart- slent is 368,408, add of these 266,550 recorded their votes. The total number polled by the candidates was :—General Boulanger, 172,272; M. Foucart, 75,181: Moreab, 6,643. - ' FURTHER RELAPSE OF THE EMPEROR FREDERICK. BERLIN, Tnowstuty, 3-40 pas.—The official bulletin, Published this afternoon, states that the Emperor Frederick's position during the put night became more favourable, and adds that the fever to-day is dimin- ished, and the general condition; better. It is never- theless thought necessary that his Majesty should re- main in bed. Bantu', THURSDAY, 3 .P.ll.—The Empqror has had ,several hours almost uninterrupted sleep, and feels in consequence stronger and Much refreshed. The feverish temperature has alp been considerably reduced: BERLIN, THURSDAY, 11..30 A.M.—According to must- worthy information the gravest fears are entertained of, a speedy fatal termination of the Emperor Frederick's illness. It is evemapprehended from the present condi- tion of the illustrious patient that the catastrophe may occur within a we& hence. A Central News telegram dated Berlin, Thursday, "--w—...12-30, says :—The 4cver has now somewhat abated, but the Emperor is very weak, and, by the advice of 'his 'Physicians, keeps his bed. His Majesty's rest was so much disturbed last night that he 4.anly obtained three- quarter of an hour's sleep. • BERLIN, THURSDAY Nnurr.— Althh late last evening the Emperor's state was pronounced to be not so good, after midnight a slight improvement occurred, and his • Majesty obtained some sleep. This morning his breath- ing was quiet4ir, but in consequence of his tempera- ture being still high he was persuaded to ,spend the day in bed. The following is this morning's bulletin :--‘4 Chariot- tenblirg, April 19, 1888. His Majesty the Emperor passed a satisfactory night. The fever is less this morning than Yesterday. The general condition is better,' bid it is desirable that kis Majesty should 'continuo to keep his bed. Morel! Mackenzie, Wegner Krause, T. Mark Hovell, Leyden, Senator." It will be observed that the bulletin makes no .reference to an affection of the lungs, of which Professor Leyden, and Senator have again to-day detected no traces. The high fever implies, however, serious mischief of some kindoand there is now, little doubt of the correctness of the announcement of, . last, night that pylenzia or blood poisoning has super- vened. The Empress Augusta. and the Crown Prince and Crown Princess were among the visitors to Charlottenburg to- day. A sympathetic crowd continues to cluster about the palace gates. ,

The first material change was to enable persons called *undertakers" to -supply municipal authorities and others with electric current without ineurring the expense and delay of getting,a special Act. Clause 7 gave power to the municipal authorities to do the,work of breaking up the streets at the cost of the suppliers of electricity, after giving due notice. Clause 10 provided that in carrying out their works the electric lighter.' should do nts injury to the existing telephone companies. rrovision was then made for payment by the electric lighting companies to the Irical authorities flr way leave of aboutT2o per mile. Then it was proposedthat at the end of five years all wires should be laid underground. With regard to the supply to the general public, the electrical undertakers were practically put under the slime conditions as gas companies, and every isliseholder 'residing within '25 yards of a distribut- ing main could demand to have an electrical supply. The bill contained provision for revocation of licenses and contracts, on application to the Board of T'radet The electrical lighting industry had been kept at a standstill by the Act of 1852, and 114 believed that if this trlll,,or someirriodification•of it, were passed, in a short, time empk)stmsnt would 'be given to 30,000 or 40,00 a persons.—Lord THURLOW, fearing that the complex bill before the House would only postpone ade.tatate legislation, was unable to Withdraw the bill which he had introduced in favour of that of the noble Earl.— The Earl of °snow said the Govirnmeht were anxious to do what they could to pmmote electrical lighting, and would not oppose the second reading of the bill, pm- vided it were referretrto a Select Committee.—The bill was•read a second time. _

The Sugar Bounties Conference again met on Monday, to elect a sub-committee to consider technical questions which had arisen at the last meeting. John Tagg, an accountant, was remanded at Glasgow. on Saturday, charged with fraud. It is alleged that he re- ceived money for ala entertainment for which no arrange- inents were made. Smith, magistrate, replyjng to the address of the solicitors present, congmtuletted Dalston on the opening of the court. • The steamer Bremen arrived at Dover on Saturday, badly damaged, having been in collision on Friday with the barque Norma, which milt. The crew of the Norms saved themselves by jumping on board the Bremen. - Three Halifax young men were rowing-in the Calder, near Brighouse, on Saturday. when the boat went over a small cataract, allied the dam stones. John William Hill, 18, was drowned, his companions gaining the shore in safety. At Stratford, Essex, on Saturday, Wm. Chilford, aged 35, was charged on remand with having, on his own con- fession. murdered Mary Taylor. about 1872, at Deeptielcl, near Wolverhampton. Trte police asked for and ob- tained a further remand, to allow of their inquiries being completed. I. , A fatal explosion occurred at Cardiff on Saturday. While the cashier was paying the men of the New Barry Railway some dynamite exploded, and hurled a mass of stone in the air. A man named Burns was killea on the spot, and anelher man had his leg broken. The cashier had a narrow escape. ' A fall of stone occurred in the Wearmouth Pits on Saturday morning. A number of men at work made a rush from the spot, but John Robson and William Reed were caught and entombed. A rescue party soon extri- cated Robson, who was severely injured, and, after working all night, Reed was found on Sunday morning, but died shortly afterwards. \ The screw steamer Levant, Captain Young, which left Cardiff on March 24 with a cargo of coal. is reported lost with all hands. THE TITBIT WAR TN WALES: EXTRAORDINARY SCENES.— On Monday, a series of extraordinary scenes charac- terised the seizure of cattle and stock for arrears of tithes at Hope, Flintshiie. Mr. l'eterson left Chester by an early train, and a large crowd speedily gathered, who celebrated the event on horns, tin pots and pans, and other unmusical instruments and implements. A black cow belonging to a widow named Braithwaite had been seized, and the lady demonstrated her aversion to the proceedings by rigging up along- side her front door two ludicrous imperpnations of the parson and the tithe - collector. Under the surplice of the clergyman was the foHowing : " Dearry beloved brethren,—lt's money I want. I must have it now. If I cannot get it, I'll sell the black cow." Mr. Peterson was apostrophised as a Shylock determined to have his pound of flesh. The cow was grazing in a field, and two emergency men seized the brute by the horns and ran it up towards the gate. Immediately a shout warraised, "Shut the gate." Mr. Peterson was, however, too sharp, and there was a heavy rapping of knuckles with stout cudgels to prevent the success of the manceuvre, and the animal was eoentually got out into the road. Here a scene of muckexcitement arose, Mr. Peterson, being surrounded by an angry crowd, ygho shouted and vociferated that he was robbing the poor widow to endow a rich institution. Offers were made to buy the cow, but Mr. Peterson, seeing the intense feeling prevailing, ordered it to be drivefi to Chester. At Mr. Swetenham's farm a haystack was seized for £23, .and the owner paid under protest. The effigies were then euried about shoulder high, and were WWl:lately beaten to pieces by the infuriattd people.

div.head: CRUEL DEIMIS OF BABIES.
div.p: CRUEL DEIMIS OF BABIES.

SHOCKING CONFESSION BY A SERVANT GIRL. At Boston (Lincolnshire), on Saturday, Alice Maud Temple, 13, domestic servant, in the employment of Joseph Gunson, farmer, of Donington Northorpe, near Spalding, was charged with attempting to suffocate Mary, Gunson, her master's child, between March 26th and the 31st.—The evidence of Mrs. Gunson was taken, and her statement was corroborated by a farmer's wife named Mary Hunter.—lnspecter Clarke stated that he took down in the presence oP a witness the following state- ment !----"lst April, 1888, Police Station, Doningten.—Alice Maud Temple. I wasl3 years of age last August. r did try 0 kill Mrs. Gunson's baby on Monday, Tuesday, Wednes- day, Thursday, and Friday in last w2elt by nipping its nose until its breath was stopped. I killed Mrs. Penny's baby, at Stanbow-lane, Boston, three weeks last Monday since in the same way. I nipped its nose until it died I afterwards told Mrs. Penny what I had done, and she told my aunt, Mrs. Priestly. lam sorry now that I did do it, but I saw Harriet Daliywater kill my little sister in the same way at No. 9. Stanbow-lane, Boston, about five years since.--Ancs Maul TENtris."—Prisoner was committed to take her trial at the forthcoming assizes.

div.head: FEARFUL TRAGEDY IN VENICE.
div.p: FEARFUL TRAGEDY IN VENICE.

One of the most &rutsl murders ever set on record in. Italy was committed last week in Venice, a city little used to —crime of such a singularly* revolting kind. Giovanni Rossi, a young arttsaai had, it seems, fallen desperately in love with is wife's sister, Anna della Giustina. As the girl steadily repulsed his advances, te conquer this absorbing passion he left Venice with his wife for 'Geno* hoping to find ' work there. In this apparently he failed; and list Tuesday returned to Venice, sending his wife to her father's house, while he went to that occupied by her sister Anna. It was early morning when he crept Up the stairs and found her alone in a 'bedroom on the fourth floor. Her brother had gone to work. Foiled hi a violent attempt upon her honour, he drew a revolver and shot her full in the face with it. Then, horribly disfigured as she was, be flung her slier over the balcony, on to the stteet pavement below. As she lay lifeless on the stones, he fled three more shots at her, and then in a frenzy of rage threw on to her body copper buckets, knives, a chopper, and everything which his madness could convert into a missile. Failing to blow out his brains with the revolver, he gashed his throat with a razor and cut open the veins of his wrists, standing out on the balcony while the blood streamed down, and calling to the horrified spectators, "E Pultimo Fatigue min ! E l'ultimo aangue ado !•" Before the police could arrive lie was a mrpse. Letters which he left upon the table show that the murder was a premeditated one, due to dishonourable passion flit his beautifnl sister-in-law. who had invariably tre6,ted him with coldness and disdain.

div.head: TETE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.
div.p: TETE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.

Speaking, an Monday. at, the annual meeting of the Hanley Liberal Council, Mr. Wodall. M.P.:said the chief defect of the Local Government Bill was that it failed to deal with the administration of the Poor Law. Whilst it constituted an authority and n'iw methods of rating, it did nothing to consolidate and unity the assessmentor collection of rates.

An adjourned meeting of chairmen and deputy-chair- men of quarter sessions was held at Ilroad Sanctuary, Westminster, on Tuesday. Sir John Dorington. M.Pc, pre- siding. Clause 18 of the Local government Bill was discusced, and approved, and a resolution passed,at the last meeting s'aiking out the licensing clauses was rescinded in faxour of a resolution expressing the opinion that it is undesirable In deal with the licensing system in the bill. Clause 20 was declared to require amend- ment. The meeting passed farther resolutions that it is Inexpedient that indoor pauperism should be the sole test for the distrbutilv of the proceeds of probate duty, and also that a inexpedient that quarter sessions, boroughs, and ountiea should be associated upon the Councils. each should collect its own duties separately. The excheauer clauses ma to 27 were then approved.
SUSPECTED ALURDER NEAR BOLTON.

On Sunday, the body of a woman, named Hodson, who lived with her husband and family in Taylor-street, Herwich, was found at the bottom of a ravine about 40ft. deep, called Johson's Clough, near that town. She had a cut on the temple and one arm was bruised. Sus- picion is directed towards a lodger named George Walker; who as seen with her on Saturday night Ho I returned home without her at a late hour, and 'after a sleep on the sufa changed his clothes and left the town. He was promptly arrested.. The clothing of George %chard Walker, iron turner, of Horwich, who was arrested on Sunday, on suspicion of murdering, at Horwich, on the previous night.", married woman, named Jane Hodson, has been examined, and blood-stains have been found on the garments. It has also been ascertained that he reached his lodgings late on Saturday night, with blood on his face,and explained the circumstances by stating that he had hdd a fight. The parties were drinking together the whole or Saturday afternoon, and were last seen in an intoxicated condition, about eight o'clock, near Jepson's Clough, a deep ravine, at the bottoln of which, 12 hours later, the dead body of tho woman was 'found, having a large wound on her head, and a punctured wound on one of her arms. The murdered woman was the wife of an Iron-turner, "and has left six children. Her husband, owing to heart disiase, has not worked for a king time. Walker belongs to Sheffield, but had lodged in the houss of the Hodsons.

The prisoner Walker was charged before the county magistrates, on Monday, with causing the death of the woman Hodson. Supt. Eatough explained the cir- cumstances of the case, and stated that as yet the police had not had sufficient time to gather evidence together. All he could du was to ask for wremand until to-morrow, The anblication was granted.

The mackerel. fishery of the south coast of frelawb has been more successful during the past few nights and. large catches are reported. At Lixnaw Chapel, on Sunday. Nora Fitzmaurice, whose father was murdered rcrent4y—two men being under sentence of death for the crime—attended mass. A larize number of persons immediately left the &ape), &Vito the protests of the priest. Some soldiers of the Derbyshire regiment at Limerick. on Sunday, broke a number of windows with Stones, and forced their way into a house where a corpse was being; waked, aid created a disturbance. ' The police were called in, and several soldiers were arrested. The brothers Murphy, whc• were tried at the last Wicklow Assizes for the murder of Head-constable Whelehan, and An which occasion the jury disagreed,, were again plac'ed in the deck on Saturday, before Judge O'Brien. No jury was sgorn, and both the hr •I‘ers, were liberated on their own recognisances of £25 e,aca to appear if called upon. A letter was published in Belfast on Monday, from tlie Rev. P. Kelly, parish priest of Dunfanag,hy, to Sir West. Ridgway, „Irish Under Secret:lrv, in which he says that as the people in the district are in the last stage of star- vation, they cannot loneer forego the natural right which every man Ills to the fruits.of his own industry. „ oercion law, bayonets. end gaols cannot make money out, of stones or shake princinik. The clergy must,lk therefore, stand by their people in distress. Mr. Harrell, the Chief of the Dublin Police, gave evi— dence on Monday before the, Select Committee of the House of Commons which is inottirint: into the operation of the Sunday Closing Arts in Ireland. He stated that. be was opposed to the extension N. the Acts to the five large towns at present exempted. He expressed the opinion/that if Sunday closing were made compulsory in the large towns a large amount of private drinking in clubs would spring up. At Ennis, on Saturday, the hearing of the case against' Mr. Dunleavy, editor of the C/a re Independent, for assaulting a constable, was resumed. Further police evidence was taken. Mr Harrington, for prisoner, ap- plied for a summons to compel tileattendance of Colonel Turner as a witness. This was rPfuse.l. The Bench then decided that theassault was itchnical, and ordered the defendant to enter into Ins recosnisntiCeS to come up for judgment when the court opened. The dAfendant de- clined to do this, and was thereupon sentenced to four- teen days' imprisonment. the Bench declining to State the cue for a superior court... RE-ARREST or MR. W. O'BRIEN, M.P. _

- ?fr. William O'Brien, M.P.. was arres•eci oh the arrival' of the mail boat Ireland at Kingstown from Holyhead, on Saturday evening. The arrest, was effected by Inspector Cooper, of the detective denartment. accompanied by two other detectives. Mr. O'Brien, without any remon- strance, entered the carriage of the train for Dublin. which the detectives pointed out to him. There were very few persons on the platform, and/be incident gave rise to no demonstration of any kind. —Upon his arrival at Dublin, the news af Mr. O'Brien'J arrest having pre- ceded him, a considerable crowd hid collected at the station. After seeing a number of friends Mr. 'Brien was taken to the Courthouse, which adjoined the bride.. well, and w charged before 41 resident magis- trate, on th, ~oimation of a police-constable, that he did, on the Bth April, takopart in, and incited and caused to incite persons to take part in, an illegal assembly. The IX trict Inspector applied for a remand, which Was granted, until' Thursday, and Mr. O'Brien was ad- mitted to bail, himself in £2OO and two sureties in Ll-00 each. He was then escorted to Dt. Duggan's residence.

_ An inquest was opened. at Horwich, on Wednesday, respecting the death of the woman whose body was found in a dough there last Sunday morning. No light was thrown as to the manner in which the deceased met her death, and in adjourning the inquiry till next aay, the Coroner said that unless there was stronger evidence to come it seemed a hardship to keep in custody the man in whose company the woman was last seen tnt Saturday evening.

In 1847 the late Lord Lansdowne nominated him his private secretarv, and he acted in that capacity until his marriage in 1851 with the daughter,of the late Mr. Justice Wightmanrwhen he received an appointment as one of the lay inspectors of schools, unNer the Corn- *mittee of Council on Education. Mr. Arnold twain visited the Con- tinent in 1865 to procure for the Itnyal Commission on Middle-class Education information respecting foreign schools for the middle and upper classes, and published In 1867 a volume on this suhiept. In 1867 he ceased to hold the Poetry Chair at Oxford; in 1869 he received the honorary degree of Doctor of Laws from the University of Edinburgh. and in 1870 from his own University of Oxford.
