Technical Education, despite the acknowledged .clifilokllty of giving the phrase a precise definition, 18 more and more en,,03,,,rint.,,, the attention of the eosin:amity. It has been broadly described as Mat kind of training which is intended to develop dex- terity and,intelligence, and a knowledge among workers of the," why" as well as the "how" of the work in which they may be engaged. There is
1 d• , Mao' • 10% vt

a growing feeling that .something more requires te be done than is accomplished in our elementary . aehoofs, or by means of the Science and Art classes ' Ividoh have proved so useful throughout the coun- try. We might well be content to urge that this is aa age of over-pressure, and that it is not desirable 'to increase the strain; but the difficulty is that we Itt'e in competition with other nations, and must 'either keep abreast of what they are doing, or be eOntent to be left behind. It does not accord with the character and genius of the Anglo-Saxon race ' to take kindly to a beating, and it is the prospect, Wo suspect, of the possibility of such a catastrophe ' „that is so many of our commercial men ' *grapple With the problem of technical educe- ' ti"3,ita• There is no question as to, the international , if Nggle ; ithas commenced—it is being felt; and, . We would not be worsted in the encounter, 'we 1 :11.41 at least see to it that vo are 2.4 well equipped for tr contest as our competitors. The great queB- - is—where and how to begin 9—and to be able ' answer this satisfactorily, each town, having re- to its own 'trade, will . have to enter upon . , ‘"lareful preliminary inquiries, or rust the risk of a "a, start and consequent disaster. On Tues. day, 4,45 a meeting called"by the Maroe, a 'nurdber of c.,.`'ao leading inhabitants of WarringtoA were use- ;;;ll3' employed in listening to an address by .Mr. 'A, •L. SMITH, assistant secretary to the National rociation for the Promotion if 'Technical Edisca- ,„l°a• Mr. Sairrll was careful to advocate the new, ..'parture on broad grounds, and without reference ' tl fads or pet theories. It was • ,resolved, after 1 haring his address, to form an association—" to .(I°lleot information; discuss the desirability of en, llcalraging tho provision Of . such instruction, with , aPecial regard to the needs and circumstances of the town of Warrington, and- po co-operate gene- t*::llY with the National Associatien.". This was as .irr as-the.meetirig could prudently go y as a first 4._ stet), and/we are glad to see a disposition manifes- ted to proceed cautiously. '• • ~.:. [ The -speeches that were made showed that, - Fbile there was an agreement ,'as . to the 1-., ity of something being done, there was Ici , 4 likelihood of considerable divergence as to what that something' should be. For instance, Mr. WHITE, whose remarks revealed that he had en attention to the subject, hinted that he %Toed with Lord WIN3IIELEIGH in Iroking foc- .l....‘Ward to their co-operating with one of the socie- '' -,..."• in either Manchester or Liverpool rather.than s?tting up business on their own •account. Mr. 2a.NEY and Mr. FINNY, who spoke aa represen- • Ztives of school-teachers, expressed theraselver on s' other hand as feeling the need of beginning with the elementary schools. This would mean la._•-mrking., so to speak, on the spot; it precludes the 117 of relying on Manchester or Liverpool, and ve lire disposed.to think that it wx:11 be the right oia37 to go to work. The statement of the objects' the National- Association urges as the first ,z7t eatiai—,, The promntion. in our .primary soliogls prthe better training of the hand and eye, by im- tei7ecl instruction in drawing, in the elements of t„71%10e, and the elementary use of tools." It seems m 116 beyond dispute that if the teaching of technical i't aoation is to be successful as a national matter; nalst be based upon the foundations at present 1 too(' hi our ,national schools. There are already 1 1 el Illany gaps between the elementary scheol and ci highest seats of learning, It becomes the 1 di, vof the State and of each municipality to en- t.tatiV.o.lir to bridge those gaps, so that it may be Ili% ele to climb from. the lowest to the highest uontg of the ladder; and so; too, that those who do titi climb high may at least be made better teas ; better by enlarging the capacity to serve the izio.nlBelves and their country, and better by afford- 4, •i'neal- higher and more varied means of enjoy- the luxuries of life. Mr. W. D. Hotroarow . • draw. 41ariced.th‘t he could see how a knOwledge of .g and n .. ef harmony of cojours might be useful ... . ano trades but he said, "if they began to qicrtY_ti,rawing to file Cutting and wiredrawing he , loot., °" see where it would/apply." Possibly not, •it :".rig .t, the lowest features of these trades, an& thmight with equal truthbe said of " the three R's 6Y are not essential to filevatting and wiredrawing: t1.411:12.e t it is not too much to say that, if a hundred --eters wi... .. Ito could read and write were pitted '''' another hundred who were ignoratit

of these qualifications, it would be found that the most intelligent workmen were the best workmen. Besides, as Mr. HOUGHTON himself remarked, "mechanical appliances of all sorts had to be introduced to secure to the manu- facturer anything like ir margin of profit;' and who is more likely to originate these improvements than the trained and intelligent workman P But it is constantly happening that the inventive artisan who gets a notion in his head finds a diffi- culty in working it out, either to his own satisfac- tion or to that of his employer, because of -his inability to make even rudimentary drawings. His fingers are not taught to "speak," and he either remains silent or lets some designing „knave filch him of his idea, and rob him of the just reward of his own observation. We hold, therefore, with Professor Htrxi.zir that, after "the three. R's " have been mastered, drawing, properly taught, is of the highest importance. He says : I do not wish to exaggerate, but I declare to you that, in my judgment, the child who has been taught to make an accurate elevation, plan ad section of a pint pot has had an admirable training of eye and hand. lam not talking about artiste education. That is not the question.. Accuracy is the foundation, of everything else, and instruction in artistic drawing is something which maybe put off till a laten stage. But this point as to drawing and other details will be matter for further consideration; it is something to know that a beginning, liowever small, has been made in Warrington, and that henceforward, if the branch association does its duty, there will be no losing sight of the question of technical educa- tion.

ENGLAND has lost one of her greatest, if not one of her most. popular writers, by the sudden death Of MATTHEW ARNOLD. It IS particulatly sad to read of his being carried off in the plenitude of his intellectual power, and when he was in the -highest spirits at the prospect of , meeting, at Liverpool, the daughter who wag returning from the United States. Heart disease seems to have been congenital; his father and grandfather died of it. He had been warned by Sir ANDREW CLAnic that it was advisable for him to husband his strength; but,this seems to have been lost sight orwhen, as on Saturday last, in the playfulness of high spirits, he took a running jump ut a low rail near the house of the relative in Liverpool with whom he was for the time staying. There was no immediate indication of injury frsrn this exertion; but whilst out walking, nett day, he fell forward and expired almost instantaneously from failure bf the heart's action. It isi of course, impossible to say that the heart would not have failed, if he had not taken this running leap; but the presump- tion is that the sudden and extraordinary call upon its capacity disturbed the circulation to such a degree as to result in syncope and death. The lesson is a painful one; gaiety of heart is no in- dication of the structural strength of that organ. The body may i;,e willing, but when the heart is weak the voice of the physician should betheard and obeyed. Mr. MATTHEW ARNOLD maybe said to have been a writer who wrote for Writers rather than for the general public. It is as a poet that he made his mark in literature, and yet it is not too much to say that his readers as a poet are exceed- ingly limited. But his audience is "fit though few." Our system of copyright has much to do ' with a limitation of this kind. Original writers do not sufficiently trust themselves to the judgment of the masses. There was a time 'when TENNYSON was little known beyond the drawing-room; but of late years the cheap editions of his works have I caused him to become in truth the poet of the people. In this way his influence has multiplied a hundredfold; and we should be loth to believe that the change has brought less grist to the mill. Mr. ARNOLD was, perhaps, too classical in style to become really popular, yet the more he is read the more he will be appreiiated. There is some- thing of EMERSON'S calmness and , strength in his linos referring to the "clear, star-sown vault of

heaven." "But with joy the stars perform their shining, i And, the sea its Tong moon-silvered roll, , For alone they live, nor pine with noting All the fever of some differing soul." Thoughts like these are calculated to take the con- ceit out of over-blown mortals—that is if they are not beyond redemption. Again " Calm soul of all things! make it mine ,To feel, amid the city'ti jar, That there abides a peace of thine, Man did not make, and cannot mar." In the time to come, there will be fervent ad- mirers of such verse when much that Mr. ARNOLD wrote in the way of criticism will have been for- gotten. Not that he was lacking as a critic ; but it is in the nature of things with this ever-rolling and ever-6hanging sphere, tilt interest in a criticism all but ceases when that whichis ex- pounded as an opinion to-day is recognised as a fact to-morrow. The highest poetry crystalises the highest truth, and it is as a poet that Mr. M ATTHEW ARNOLD will be known to posterity.

THE Licensing Clauses of the Local Government Bill are being subjected to severe criticism, both in the House of Commons and throughout the country. Mr. Caine, who, as a Liberal. Unionist, has steadily supported the Government, has given the Ministry to understand that, if the provisions for compensation are forced through the House the issue raised will not be settled, but will afterwards be fought, tooth and nail, in every town in the Kingdom. The Solicitor-General, on Tuesday, attempted to make out a case of - vested interest on the part of pub- licans; but, unfortunately, he 'is not in a Pot ition to quote a single instance to show that the law has over recognised a vested interest. • On the contrary, Mr. JUSTICE STEPHENS, ra higher authority than the SOLICITOR-GENERAL, remarked as to the well-known Darwen appeal case, that the ILegislature "does not treat the interest as a vested one in any way." Lord HARTINOTON, in speaking, at Darwen, in 1883, made special ref erence I to the important issue then raised. His remarks as quoted by Mr. JOHN MoRLEY, at Darweh, on Wednesday, were :.--" I believe this decision goes to show /that the licensing justices have now under the present law full discretion not only as to the granting of new licences, but as to the renewal of old ones. That is a decision of very great im- portance. ,It tOuches very closely the question of compensation. This decision, will have a strong effect on the opinion and the tactics of the licensed victuallers, and will make them more dis- posed to the reasonable proposals which may now be made, and to .Iccept a reasonable compromise, which, if they resist too long, may be no longer within their reach." It is to be hoped that Lord HaariNorox is still in the same frame of mind, and that he will act in the spirit of the decision to which he justly atta:ched so much importance. If the Bill should pass as it stands, the ratepayers , will discover, too late, their liability to be robbed in a wholesale fashion. At a meeting ef the licensed victuallers of Manchester and Salford, held on Wednesday, Mr. C. H. M. WHARTON let the, cat out of•the bag. Re said "the bill was a ; very good one in the interests of the licensed vie- ;

He may have said this with reference to the opening field for disputes and appeals rather than with an eye to compensa- tion.. But the bill is in the interests of licensed victuallers; it is not in the interests of ratepayers, asithey will find to their cost, if these clauses be- come lava'. The _scheme is one, as Sir WILFRID Levisox has described it, to endow decayed pub- licans. We have endowed the Church, and we are now being called upon to endow the Beer- batrel.
LOCAL NEWS.

NOR RATE 'FOR NORTON.—The Runcorn magistrates on Monday sanctioned the laying of a poor rate for Nor- ton of is in the £ for the next six months. The rate is estimated to realise £336 12s Etd. . DISTRICT RATE FOR RuNcouN. At a special meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, on Monday evening, Mr. J. Dobson presiding, the seal of the Board was affixed to a general district rates of 24 in £ for the year ending the 25th March, 1889. THE MURDEROUS ASSAULT DY A SOLDIER AT WIDNES.— Daniel Gilmour, a discharged soldier, was again brought before the Widnes magistrates, on Monday, charged with wounding Joseph Donovan, with intent to murder him—Superintendent Johnstone said the injured man was still unable to appear, and the prisoner was accord- ingly remanded until Monday nexl. WIDNES c.E.T.S.—In connection with this society the Rev. J. R. Jones, curate, gave a lecture in the Natipnal Schools, on Thursday evening. There was a good atten- dance, and the Vicar (the Rev. S. Wright Williams), pre- sided. The subject of the lecture was "Cathedral,: and abbeys," and it was rendered highly interesting by means of numerous limelight views shown by Mr. J. IL

Imison. . ALBERT-ROAD WESLEYAN SCHOOL, WIDNEM. --• The an- niversary services in aid of this school were held on Sun- day, and good congregations assembled at both the morn- ing and evening services to listen to the discourses of the Rev: A. Percy Watson, of Runcorn. In the'afternoon an address was delivered to parents and scholars; The chdir and children saw, music specially selected. A col- lection was made at each service. SERVICE OF SONG AT WIDNES. The choir of Zion Chapel, Widnes, on Saturday evening gave the Service of Song entitled "The Resurraction." The service of song, , which was compiled by the Rev. R. Lowry specially for 1 E'aster, consists of scripture readings with responses; in- terspersed With suitable choruses and hymns. lirt. J. Betney, senr., conducted the choir with his-accustomed ability, and Mr. A. Ogden ably accompanied. The Rev. El Hall, the pastel., was the reader. REMANDED AT WIDNES.—LaW/BLICe Moran, a r gatherer, who has taken up his residence at the Model Lodging-house, was charged with stealing a coat, worth Bd, the property of John Newell, of 36, Dixon-st. .The prisoner wak remanded until Monday. Wm. Curwin, a boy, of 14, Peel-st. was also remanded on a charge of stealing a padlock and key, the property of John Barber, of Lacev-st.—Williarn Derrnott, a middle-aged man, was charged with having, on the 17th April, been drunk and disorderly in Wellington-st., and also with assaulting P.C. Houghton. Theprisoner, who had kicked the officer very severely about the legs, was remanded until Thurs- day. SEHMOM TO RAILWAY-MEN AT WIDNES. Out of res- pect to the memory of William Davies, the shunter, who was killbd:at Widnes.. on Saturday, the 7th inst., about 300 of tlie.employe.s of the London and North-Western . Railway Company, assembled at the house of the parents of their uidertunate comrade on Sunday afternoon. [Here they formed aprocession and walked to St. Mary's Parish Church, where the vicar, the Rev. J. Wright. Williams preached an eloquent sermon with special refe- - rene.e to the sad event. His solemn words of encourage- ment and warning Were listened to witli close atten- tion. ' 1 AN UNDESIRABLE CUSTOMER AT WIDNES.—JOIIIIPonnor, ' ' of 47, Lacey-st.,was brought up at Widnes Police Court, on Monday. to answer a charge of being drunk and dis- orderly, and also of assaulting Ann Lynch, wife of a shopkeeper in Newtown. The prisoner, whilst In a state of drunklenness, entered Lynch's shop on Saturdgy night, and demanded some beer, and because Mrs. Lylich said td she could not supply his wants, but would give him some "pop," he declar he would hive her life. As an earnest of his intentions e followed the woman into the kit‘chen, , but her screams brought down her husband from the . bedroom, and the prisoner was given into custody. The prisoner informed Mr. Bmck that he had not the ilightest recollection of the occurrence. He was fined 5s and costs for being drunk, and as Mrs. Lynch did not wish to press her charge, that case was dismissed on the pay- ment of costs. , BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN THPROVENENT .CLASS, RUN- conic—The members of this class passed a pleasant even- ing :with Ireland's National Bard—Tom Moore—on Wed- nesday evening. There was a good attendance, and the followir7 programme was gone through in capital styki : —Opening hymn, “Ifyriam?'s Song,"" Memoir of Moore," Mr. T. Leach; song' "The Harp of Tara," Mr. R. Moore; reading,. "The Looking Glass," Mr. Wardle; song, "The Minstrel Boy," Mr. R. Morris; pianoforte solo "The last rose of summer," Mr. C. C. LeCouteur ; Paradise and Pen "Introduction," Mr G. A. Hayes; "The Blood," Mr..Palin ; "The Sigh," Mr. C Norman; "The Tear," Mr. w. Millington; " L'envol," Mr. G. Hayes; song, "Believe me if those endearing young charms," Mr. Williams ; ballad, "Lake of the dismal swamp," Mr. F. Eden; song, "Let Erin remember the days," Mr. R. Moore; critique on Moore's poetry, Mr. W. Millington. Mt. T. Simister, the president, occ the chair, and Mi.. T Breach, was the accompanist. 1

ATTACKED BY A WOMAN AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. J. Brock and Mr. H. Gaskeli, junr., at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, a married woman named Ann Robinspn was charged with assaulting George Jackson, a labourer, who resides in Marsh-st.. It appeared that OD Saturday night Jackson was having a drink at the Central Hotel bar, when he heard the prisoner say to some men," That is him who got my chap fourteen days," at the same time making use of oaths. The. prisoner `ollowecl Jackson into the street, and having handed to a companion some artificial flowers that she was carrying for sale, she at- tacked him, and: a; man who wat with her lent his help by knocking him to the ground. The prisoner then kicked him on' the cheek, and twice bit his little finger very savagely.' There were three serious wounds-on his tin- gets, and Dr. Hutchinson was attending to them. The only reason he could assign, for the woman's conduct was that her husband was sent to gaol for fourteen days for an assault upon him.—The prisoner was remanded for a week. _

DESTRUCTTCE FEMALES AT Wineiss.At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursdkry,Catherine Hynd, of 7, Marsh-st., was charged with having, err the 16th Inst., created a a disturbance in. Water-at., and also with having wil- fully broken eleven panes of glass in a house in that street, of which Daniel Lowry was the agent, and done other damage amounting in all to £l. Prisoner pleaded guilty, and was fined 2s 6d and costs, 7s 6d, and ordered to pay the amount of the damage. - She WM also or 7 dered to be bound over for six months, or go to gaol for seven days. Mary Jane Riley, aged 15 years, whose home is at 22,.Water-st„ was Charged with having, on the 15th inst., broken two panes of glass and damaged the sash of a house in Sankey-, for which Daniel Lowry is agent. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and Vas ordered to pay 14s, or go to gaol for seven days.—Ellen Whittle. a young woman. was charged with having committed a breach of the peace in Water-st. me the 9,th April, and with lor},aking twelve panes of glass in the-house of Ann Dodd, Sankey-st. In default of paying a fine of 17s in. chiding costs, and finding sureties for hergood behaviour for six months, the prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was sent to gaol for fourteen. days. DROWNED IN DITTON BROM—A drowning accident of a sad character occurred at Ditton on Sunday. About three o'clock lin the afternoon a fireman named 'John William Fay; who lives. at Wood's cottages, had his atten- tion drawn to a frock in Ditton Brook a few hundred yards above the railway. He managed to drag it to the ' bank, and then discovered that it enclosed the logiFly of James Alfred Lea. aged 2i years, son of the landlord of the Railway Hotel. In the hope that life might not, be altogether extinct. Fey held the child upside down, and then rolled him upon the bank, but without result. The brook runs along side the Railway Hotel, and it is suP- posed that the child had been playing about, and having scrambled through the railings that fenced the brook., had fallen into the water and been carried away by the. receding.tide. Mr W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner; on Tuesday afternoon held an inquest upon the body, and he instructed Fay in future not to act as he had done in this instance, but to lay the drowning person upon his back, and, pressing upon his chest, work both arms slowly up and down. The coroper also remarked that had there been a garden beyond the fence instead of a brook the owneratould have put up such a fence that not even a hen could have got through; they would not take the same precaution for a little ,ehild.—MrLeather (a juryman) said there. was a 'strong high fCnce of sleepers up to the Railway Hotel, and then there was an ordinary fence. He suggested that the sleeper fence should be extended to the roadway.—A „presentment to this effect was added to the verdict of "Accidentally drowped," and the Coroner said he would communicate with fhe London and North-Western Railway Company, and do what he could to carry out the views of the ' jury. „ THE ALLEGATION AGAINST A WIDNES POLICENAN.— Alice Hatton, oc 53. James-st., was again brought up at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, to answer a charge of being drunk anddisordorly- on the 31st March. About a quarter-past eleven on the night of the date mentioned P.C. Holbrook found the prisoner in a state of intoxica- tion at West Bank Docks uI da,ngtr of lalling in the. water. She was accompanied by a flatman named John Shaw, who stated he was going to take her on the flat for safety. The constable took the woman to her home, but her 'husband refused to allow' her to enter the hoese, and some neighoours took care of her. At the last court the woman accused the constable of haling made im- proper overtures to her. Mr. William Hem's- Breeden., a schoolmaster, now came forward, and stated that lie was with the officer at the time, and the accusation was false. The woman was 'very drunk..,-Catherine Edwards, of James-st., said the prisoner was "very full" indeed. The prisoner was fined 103 and costs, and the witnosses were allowed expenses.--David Hatton, the husband of the prisoner in the last case, was charged with creating a brearh of the peace on the game night. The defendant whendds name was called out, replied in a loud voice, " Hear," and jumping upon the defendant's box, gave a short step dance, and amid the laughter of the court ejaculated " Give me seven years while you are agate pf me." P.C. Holbrook then described how the defendant refused td have his wife in the house, and threatened to split the constable's head open with a poker he carried if he did not go away. He made such a noise that he 'caused all the neighbours to assemble in the street. Catherine Edwards gave corrobative evidence, and the defendant shouted that ",She wanted a rope round her neck." ' He was bound over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO and two sureties of £5 each.

RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY, COMMITTEE. - The annual financial statement of the Free Library has just beensub- mitted by Mr. J. D. Jones, the librarian. The income for the year, including £lBO les from the rates, amoun- ted to t 26964 7d. The expenditure amounted to £268 1.6 s 10d, and included salary, £5O, new books, £73 17s 7d, magazines, Ace., £22 2s 9d, binding, £3O es 3d, and fittings, £53 2s 7d. There was a balance of 9s 9d to be carried forward. During the past month there had been 2,558 books issued from the Library, an increase of 405 as Compared with the corresponding period last year. "REMEMBER Noirrnwicu. '—A few days ago a Run- corn gentleman addressed a communication to Sir Wil- liam Harcourt, pointing out that in his recent speeches at Derby and York he had, when dealing with the bye- elections, omitted to mention the great victory in the I Northwich Division, a minority of 458 being converted ' into a majority of 1,129. The follpwing reply has been received :—" Malwood, Lyndhurst. April 17, 1888. Dear sir. It must be an error of the reporters if the, mention of Northwich was omitted. You may be skire I never fail to 'Remember Northwich.'—Yours truly, W. V. ilia- conny." ' _

Routint AT WIDNES.—James Mistleroaged 15 years was brought before Mr. John Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, charged with stealing three india rubber rings or buffers from railway waggons, the property of Messrs. James Muspratt and Sons, and also with stealing an india rubber buffer from a waggon be- longing to the Garswood Coal and Iron Co. The rings were identified, and it was proved that the prnoner had sold them along with others to Mrs, Ann Simcock, marine store dealer, 5, Appleton-st., Widnes.. He-received ten- pence for the lot. The prisoner plWed guilty, and was lined lfis in each case. .

" SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNP.S.—George Hyland, aged 20 years, who was a labourer, and had resided at 1, Ger- rard-st , died suddenly on Tuesday afternoon. On Mon- day morning Hyland complained of pains in his head and , bock, and in the evening Dr. Hutchinsod saw him and prescribed for him. When the doctor called again next morning his patient was in a start of collapse, and death took place at half-past one. Thterday afternoon, Mr. Drthouse held an inquest upon the body;--Dr. Hutchin- son, who had made a post-mortem examirsatiem, pro- nounced death to be due to congestion of the lungs, and a verdict was returned accordingly. Tax Iloint hum TRADE.—The English iron mar- ket its quieter in its aspect this week. This is stated to be due chiefly to the unsettled state of matters on therCbntinent, and not to any weakness of the iron ' trade: People hesitate at present in placing orders, the prevailing- uncertainty tending to check opera- tions.. Prices, on tl€ whole, continue to be steady, and those for pig-iron may even be saidt to be stronger. Manufactured iron, on the contrary, is easier.. Mere are not many new orders coming fmt ward;.ane the quarterly meetings have been rather 'disappointing—lies. PAILIINP. OVA LOCAL COLLIERY PROPRIETOR.— At a meeting of the creditors of William Smethurst. colliery proprietor, Brynn, near Wigan, held on Saturday at Nottingham, the liabilities were stated at ..£2LOOO. The debtor was left by his father the Garswood .Hall Colliery, Lancashire, which was turned ' into a company. He afterwards became proprietorof the Theatre Royal, Wigan, and at the time of his failure was connected with the Granst Theatre, Nottingham. He was a witness in th 4 Ellis-Lever case. He attributed his failure to the depressed condition of the coal trade. Tito Official Receiver said the case was ailiad one, and required search ing investigati on. ' • TASHION'ABLN MARRIAGE IN CHESHIRE. ThO marriage between Mr. G. W. Duff Assheton-Smith. Vaynol Park, Bangor, and Miss Laura Alice Jones, the•youngest daughter of Mr. Colin Stanhope Jones, St. George's-square, London, was solemnised on, Thursday, at Broxton, Cheshira. The event is being celebrated a ith many demonstrations of joy throughout North Wales, where Mr. Asslicton- Smith possesses extensive slate quarries, as well as large estates. Mr. Assheton-Sraith is returning to his tenante the whole of the half-year's rent, the value of the gift representing .£14,000. • The gar- deners, gamekeepers, and woodmen on .the Vaynol Park estate,together with the wigole of the slate quarrymen. with their wives and children, have been presented with railway passes to Liverpool and Manchester. LIVERPOOL. ENGINEERING .SOCIETY.—The usual

_ fortnightiv.meeting of the Liverpool Engineering Society was held at the Royal Institution, ,Colquitt- street, on Monday evening, wen a paper on" Steam Boiler Explosions, was read by Mr. John J. Web- ster, M.lnst. CH.,end discussed by the members'. The paper commenced tiyatating, that the average number of steam boiler explosions during the last 25 years is about 5d per annum, the average loss of life amounting to. about 70 per annum; and although the number of ,explosions is very great, and the loss of life to be deplored, the actual per ceutage of explo- sions to boilers at work is vert small, being at the rate of one explosion to every 2,500 boilers at work. Owing to the•good work of the different Boiler As- sociations, and to. the immense improvement in the design and construction of boilers, this per centage has now, been reduced to lesi than one in ".apoo. The paper described in detail the various causes of boiler explbsions, and was illestrated by numerous diagrams.. The farther discussion was adjourned. NIABILL4.OB OP . TUB HON. It. The District Attendance Committee reported that dur- ing March school fees had been paid in 20 cases, and 01 persons had been summoned beton the Committee for contravention of the Education Act, fifty-fOor of whom were brought before the magistrates and convicted. ran sTARDAno OF EXEMPTION. Mr. Deacon regorted That the District Education Com- mittee and the School Management Committee had had a conference as to the standard of exemption, and they had weed that a child between-ten and thirteen years of age should not be required to attend •School if such child had roceived a eertiflca,te from one of Her Majesty's Inspectors of Schools that it had reached the sixth stan- dard, prescribed by the code of 11376.--Mr. Deacon said

the ordinary standard wa the siktii, but the recom- mendation of the committ?,e gave the Board power .to allow a child to leave school when it had reached the fifth standard, if they were satisfied it was properly em- ployed either at home or elsewhere. He thought this would work well. The recommendation was passed. AN APPOINTMIZNT.

On the proposition of the Sch&A Management Com- mittee, the tender of Messrs. John Heywood and Co. for the supply of dual desks for the Board schools was ac- cepted, and Win. Henry Parsons was appointed caretaker and cleaner of Warrington-road schools, at a salary of £1 per week, with residence, taxes, water, coal, and gas free.

_ Thursday l _ Ist was Primrose Day; and the buttonholes of ConservatiVes were quite gay. They still rejoice on the anniversary of the ° death of Lord Beaconsfield.

Mr. W. O'Brien has been again arrested; and now it is Mr. John Dillon's 'turn. This is the Irish Secretary's way of settling the Jrish ques- tion. Mrs_Partington goes to the sea shore' trundles her mop, and vows she is keeping back the Atlantic: Such is the wisdom with which Ire- land is governed.

It is to be hoped that there is no trUth in the rumour that the eldest son of the Comte de Paris is to be offered a post in the English army. Apart from the irritation it would cause the French, it would not be.good policy towards the English. It is quite enough to have German leeches fastening upon us; if French specimens. are also to be given a turnj we shall aopn have to write up—" No Eng- -11811 need apply."

Orange peel has ita uses, but it is out of place on the pavement; and, as it is an offence against the law, the police authorities of S. Helens have determined that offenders shall be brought to a , knowledge of the error of their ways. Two per- sons have been brought before the magistrates, and dismissed with a caution'. The nuisance -would soon be abated if other authorities would follow this laudable example.

John Troy i was brought before the Warrington County magistrates, on Wednesday, for being con- cerned n what seems to have been a prize fight on Sunday last. It is as well to 'keep vp old associa- tions; there was some hard figntmg at a place called Troy some years ago.. It vitp prize-fighting, too, the prize in that case being echarming crea- ture ramed Helen we forget her "other name." It is stated that the prize fought for on Sunday was one of filthy lucre. These are degenerate days. .

Thomas Allen' the Southport policeman, who while'cn.his beat one night broke the window of a jeweller's shop and stole a large number of watches and rings, doubtless thought he likd done a clever thing; but it was very stupid of hip to proceed to pawning and selling the property m the same town. It is well that hewas thus stupid; he was the molt readily found out. Five years' penkl servitude is a serious sentence; but hi§offence was a serious one; he was engaged to protect the pro- perty which he appropriated.

The feeling is almost universal that the War Office has stupidly blundered in court-martialing Major .Templer for alleged betrayal of military secrets. Thbre was nothing • like a case against him, and with due investigation this would have been permitted before an inquiry was proposed. Mijor Templer comes off scot free ;it is the War Office that is discredited. Our "secrets "—save the mark !—are well known; and other nations are laughing at us.. Lord Randolph Churchill has said some strong things about the way we have in the arm;', but not a bit too strong.

The bi-annual curling tournament for the Hoj2 den sterling Silver Challenge Shield, value fifty guineas, and other prizes, commenced at the South- port Glaciarium on Tuesday morning; in the pre- sence of a fair assemblage of spectators, It is curious.to think of this sport upon the ice in con- nection with the advance of spring; but it is more than curious—it is a delightfully coolproceed- ing to enter the Glaciarium on a hot summer day. Try it, next time you are. in Southport, with a thermometer over 70; you will like it.

A J.P.'ship has its duties as well as its honours; but this fact seems to be disregarded by the magistrates of 'the Prescot district. On Tuesday, the business of the Police Court had to be ad- journed for "another fortnight" &wing to the abence of a second magistrate. Thomas Bellis, chlrged with the theft of a garden spade and fork had for a second time to be remanded in conse- quence of the negligence of the great unpaid. This is not justice. If the magistrates will not do the work, would it not be as well to give •them the sacks

Our neutral contemporary, after the fashion of its old braggart days, has been boasting that its circulation is many times greater than all the local papers combined. It will be seen from another column that we challenge the "Warrington Guar- than" to show that it has a local circulation as large even as our own. On Monday, at the auction of papers at the Warrington Co-operative Society, ,the "Guardian," costing 3d. weekly for Wednes- day's and Saturday's issue, fetched 7d. for the quarter; the "Examiner," costing id. weekly, realised Ad. for the qaarter. We leave the reader to point his 'own moral.

.1 The Convocation of York has been protesting in its obstinate, muddle-headed, fashion against the proposal to legalise marriage with a deceased's wife's sister after .the -manner of other rational communities. The bishops have been beaten out of the scriptural argument, and Lord Chancellor Espin now says "the object of many who sup- ported the bill was to set the Church and State by the ears." He does not see that it is clerical re- sistance to common sense whiCh seta the Church and State by the ears. If it had not been for the opposition of the bishops 'in the House of Lords,the bill would have become law years ago.

The Government are rushing the Local Govern- ment Bill through with all the speed possible, and Conservatives even are disposed to protest at private members' nights being appropriated with that object. Mr. Seton-Karr, the member for St. Helens, and Mr. Jennings' the member for Stock- port, both entered a protest in the debate on the' subject raised the other evening by Mr. Lftbou- chere. The tact is the public, if Parliament does not give the matter due consideration, will find , themselves saddled with a measure hich is as bad as'bad can be in some particulars. There is too much in it of the spirit of the old rhyme : • Taklng back and giving— Old Nick's living.

Active steps are being ,taken to fittingly com- memorate in July of tins year, the tereentenarY of the defeat, of the Spanish Armada, _in 1588: The celebration ought to be made a truly national one, for it is pleasant to remember that, although King Philip proposed to take possession of England as a Catholic, with the special sanction of the Pope, English Catholics showed themselves on the occasion to be stout 'patriots, and volunteered in large numbers to serve Queen and Country. Eliza- beth as we know, proudly acknowledged their loyalty. • Macmillan's Illustrated "English Magazine". for April, has an exceedingly interesting article 'on th 6 Armada) and reproduces platei of some of the tapestry hangings of the House of Lords, "repro- seating the several engagements between the Eng- lish and Spanish Fleets." These plates are of special value, from the fact that the tapestry was destroyed in the great fire of 1834. Mr. Austin Dobson, it may be added, has a ballad on the Armada, one verse of which runs as follows : King Philip had vaunted his claims: - - And had sworn for a year he would sack us, • With an army of heathenish names He was going to fagot and stack us. Like thieves ot the sea he would triter us, And shade, our ships on the main,. But *e had bold Neptune to back us,— And where are the galleons of Spain?

div.p: FINANCE.-BORROWED MAICEY.

The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for the past month amounted to. £193 Os 9d, and recom- mended the payment of accounts amounting to £BlO 19s 2d. It was also recommended that the committee be empowered to obtain a loan of £4,000 from the Public Works Loan Commissioners for the additional accommo- dation required at Simms Cross, Warringtowroad, and ' West Bank schools for fifty years at 3gt per cent.—Mr. Ilexes moved the adoption of the minute.—The Chkir- mansaidthe Government had recently launched a financial scheme by which they were going to borrow on loWer terms than they had hitherto done. It seemed to him I that Government should lend out money at the same rate at which they received it. He • suggested that before this recommenda- tion was passed thatthe committee should inquire from the Public Works Loan Commissioners whether therewas to be any alteration in the rate of interest in the future. —This suggestion was agreed to, and the minutes were passed with that exception. •

Captain Wareing said that at the request Of Dr. O'Keeffe, he had t 6 bring before the Board the subject of some remarks made by Mr. James White at the annual vestry meeting on the 28th March.—Mr. White said he was sorry that for the ensuing year the overseers would have M increase the rate from 2.s in the £ to 23 4d in the £. This increase; he alleged, was entirely owing to the increased demand of the School Board. The School Board for next year had demanded an increase of £7OO. on last year. The facts briefly stated were these: The addition to the.precept of the Board was £7OO. A penny in the £ on the.rateable value would produce £544, nil if they added to that sum the balance the overseers had in hand, £431, that made a total of £975. Deduct £7OO thatthe School Board required,* and the overseers were leftwith £275 for contingencies. That would meanithat a rate of 2s id would meet all the requirements, whereas the overseers had laid a rate of as 4d. A rate of 4cl in the Z'avould produce £2,160, therefore the overseers had asked for £1,580 more than was necessaryto meet the ex- ' tra 'all of the School Board.—Mr. White had spbmitted that a rate of 2s in the £ would have been sufficient had it not been for this additional call.—The Chairman said he was very much obliged to Mr. Wareing for making this statement. They had been called an extravagant Board, and it was well that the ratepayers should have • the true facts placed before them. -

, MIL MITSPRATT ON LOCAL TAXATION. .; The third. of a series of papers on political ques- tions was- read before the members of Widnes Liberal Club‘ on Monday evening by Mr. H. B. Shores. Liberal. agent to the Division. who had chosender his subject,.•`The Local Government Bill and its relation I* Lancashire"' There was a good attendance, and Mr. E. K. Muspratt, J.P., occupied the chair.—The Chairman,.in opening the proceed- ings, said although the Local Government Bill was a very great advance upon bills! that had been formerly Introduced, principally by Conservative Grovemmenta, still there were many defects in the bill, and many things with which he could not agreee. NA, that we were approaching a settlement of the great ' question of Local Government for England for the first time for many years, it was desirablethat the Act when should be one which mould satisfy the country passed should anyirate ageneration—(applause)--and no Act of Par- liament could satisfy the country unless it was founded entirely upon justice to all partiesi (Hear, hear.) The County Councils, as they knew. were to have recourse to taxation; and if that taaationwas unjust, they might depend maw it there wouldtarise a. feeling in the country against the Act, and there would be continued discus- sion .andthe question would not be settled satisfac- torily. Goschen, who, perhapismore than any other member of Parliament, had considered this question, made a report in 1871, in which he pointed out that whenever the question came before the country there must be a re-adjustment of taxation. He (Mr. Mus- pratt) thought it was. important that when the new County Councils were formed that the taxes which they raised should be equal upon, everody as far as pos- sible, . and. also that every person should con- tribute to . the government of the country in proportion, to his means. (Hear. hear.) Now 30 or 40 years age the land in.Widnes had only an agri- cultural value; but the toil Of. the people and the works of the manufacturers had enhanced the value of that land to.an.immense extent,.and yet while the manufac- turers and:other people had.contritrated to the local ex- penditure of Widnes through, the local rates in order to carry out sanitary improvementa and to support the poor, the owners ot land,lfAhe land was not built upon, had not contributed one farthing.. Was that right; was, it just 7' ('Shame;") Mr. (ioschen ought to devise sow means by which land of/ that:character should con- tribate to the expenditure . of the • neighbourhood--;-(ap- plause)—and yet in. this, bill he made no proposal to carry out that which he said cfns ,Inly just 18 years ago, that the rates should be divided between landlord and tenant. Alluding to subventiOns to local taxation from Imperial taxation Mr. Muspratt condemned the system as bad in principle, not onlp because it was unjust be- cause theincidence of taxation was unjust, but because it contributed towards extravagant expenditure. This Mr. Gosehen. thorouthly-recogiused, and he said he was going to do away with these.subrentions to particular local expenditure, but all he did was to change its character. . Be was not going to give a grant to con- stabulary, but he would give.the produce of certain Im- perial taxes to the new County: Councils. That seemed to him.(Mr. Muspratt) to.-he' very little improvement. As to the suggestion to make • personal property contri, bete towards local rates, the e-xperience of wry county that had tried it was that- it antis practicallrimpossible. After axeference to the ineqyallty and injustice of the death duties. Mr. Muspratt condemned the proposed tax on wheels as an hindrance • to trade and industry, and Said it was far better that the ratepayers should pay a 'little more to rates than submit to this impediment to the trade of the country. Althetigh this County Govern- ment Bill might be a thoroughly Ttemocmtic Bill, he was sorry. to see a provisien that these should be "selected councillors" or in ether wont& Aldermen, who had been the cause of so much diffitulty in the administration of municipal affairs. LiberaWandTorien ought to accept the principle that lay at the bottom of the Bill, and insist that the new-county councils: shall be elected solely by the ratepayers. (Applause.)., , Mr. Shores then read Ins.papex, and at the outset gave a brief.liistorical account of existing local bodies. The Widnes division in 1881 contained 9,488 inhabited houses antapepulation of 5319.51 persons, and the unfortunate inhabitants were •veryy much governed by the following authorities :—The counts.- bench of quarter sessions, 5 local.beards, 2 boards. el ournlians, 2 rural sanitark authorities, 1 highway laaa'ad. 1 school board,. 3 school attendance committoes. and 29 overseers. These authorities wereelectedthyseveral distinct methods of vot- ing upon different cla tes and for varying terms of office, and their powers of taxation. were almost as varied. For the evils consequent on sucha complicated system there was ,but, one remedy7-consolidation.. Mr. ports then des- cribe.d the con Aitution of the proposed county councils, and tho district ' councils, and the process -by which the members would be elec- ted, and also, their powers of administration.. In Lancashire. he Said. 'With its 31 millions of people, its 30. unions, its 751:mogisi-rates, and its 33 petty sessional divisions, they should demand a!sub-division of the .county, say into,north, south-west, and south-east, with. , separate lord lieutenancies, and benches of quarter ses- sions at Liverpool. Lancaster, and Manchester. Lanca- shire, if undivided, would confer upon its inhabitants a. 'franchise vastly inferior to t,hat of other counties, and it behoved Lancashire ratepayers. Liberal and Tore alike, I to take some steps to prevent the threatened Tory don of their v,oting strength. In. conclusion, the.con• • solidation that. was so much needed was conspicuous by its absence from the Bill. The Guardians would still continue tomcercise their ftinctions in the adminiatmtion, of the poor law; Education Boards would continue as at " present under a variety of authorities; whilst the.over- ' seers, with. thefr curious obsolete methods or elections were still rrpetuate.d. On the motion of Mr'.• Carer seconded by Mt. Haat- land, a. cordiff vote of tit-Ilk-3 was accorded to Mi. Shores far Ms paper, and P 'similar vote having been passed ta the chairman, the proceedings terminated.

APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN. The Clerk announced that the first business was the appointment of a chairman for ti.e ensuing year.—Mr. Handley said he had great pleasure in proposing that Mr. Gassage take the chair for the coming year. They had had Mr. Go.ssag•rs services in the past, and they had given satisfaction to the whole of the mem- bers.—Mr. Sadler seconded the motion with plea- sure, and it was carried by acclammation.—Mr. (ios.sage then took the chair, and said that he had hid such pleasure in being chairman in the past that it wouldbe ungraceful on his part if he did not again accept the appointment and thank them. The members had treated him with univer4ll kindness and courtesy, and with their assistance. the business of the Board had been well eOnducted. • THE COmmiTTEEs. Mr. Brown moved that for the next year there be six committees instead of five, and that anew committee, to be called- the Hospitals Committee, be formed. He

(argued that at present the Health Committee had too much work underits control.—Mr. Gaskell seconded the proposition, and stated that in support of his action that during the last two years the death rate had increased 50 per cent. In 1885 the death rate' was 16.62 ; in 1886 it was 2196 ; and in 1887 the death rate N,'s 23.23. In the . face of .. ... . . .

• figures like those it was evident that the work of the ' Health Committee was too great, and he was afraid that it would be greater in the future, because-they were( not doing leseln connection with the sanitary condition of the town, but much more.—Dr. O'Keeffe contended that the Health Committee had performed its functions quite as efficiently as any other committee. Because the Gas and Water Committee had failed in a artain tran- saction that it had recently undertaken he did "not see why the chairman of that committee should casttoppro- brium upon the Health Committee, because the death rate was 23 per thousand last year. There was an unusually dry summer, and the amount of diarrhcea and dysentery that prevailed in the township was suf- ficient to account for the higher death rate. He did net think that the higher death rate was owing to the in- efficient manner in which the 'scavenging was done.; the work 'of the committee was in no way neglected. The members of the committee were anxious to carry out the work in the most efficient manner, and it lutist be borne in mind that: the committee had lost the services of one gentleman' for nearly twelve months, and even if they could not get certain "cheap matters" from him might have aided them with his advice on sanitary matters. Mr. Carey said there was now a possibility of doing. what the Board petitioned the Cheshire Lines to do some- time ago—that was tef have a passenger station at Moss. Bank.. The local trains on the Cheshire .Lines that now stopped' at Widnes, could then stop at Moss Bank. Efe. understood that there was a building suitable for the pur- pose available, and which would not be available at some. I futu'reffme. He proposed that a resolution be pissed to the effect that the Board considered that a station at Moas. Bank would be a benefit to the public of Widnes. In the neighbourhood of the proposed station there Were 1,400 liouses, and at 5i persons per house, which was about the average for Widnes, gave a population.of 8,000. —Mi. NIVATES.—The master of the workhouse reported therawere 496 inmates in the workhouse this week, 505 in the preceding week, and 4611 in the corres- ponding period last year. There had been 94 vagrants relieved during the week, against 67 in the correspond- ing period last year. 'Fun RkTNFORD Emcnos.—The Clerk reported that Mr. Edward Birchall, Reed's-brow, Rainford; was the only gentleman nominated as the Guardian for Rainford, and he had been declared elected.
- PRESENTATTONS.—The Workhouse Ma9ter reported that Mr. W: B. Longton had sent A number of illustrated books and•papers for the use of the inmates, and thanks were tendered to the donor. _ . _

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess. I VIOLENT Te.sxr.—For having been drunk, and Apr , begging in Knutsford-road, on the previous night, John Jones, a tramp, was sent to prison for 14 days' hard labour. The Chief- Constable (Mr. Hunt) stated that the prisoner was very violent when brought to the police station and rent his clothes into shreds. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Alder- , men Davies' and Harrison, and Councillor J. Greening and John Pierpoint. DRITNICENNESS.—The following persons were dealt With for this offence :—Elizabeth Harrison, in Sankey-street, on Saturday, discharged on promising to leave the town; William Yates, in the Market Hall, on Saturday night, sent to gaol for a month with hard labour • 'Herbert Woods, in Bridge-street, on Saturday night, fined ss, in- cluding costs; Michael Morris, in Wilderspool-road, on Sunday night, fined 5s and costs • Elizabeth Edwards, in King-st., on the 7th of April, fined ss, including costs; Hugh Jones, in Queen-st., on the Same date, fined ss, including costs. BREACHES OF BYE-LAWS.—For having the chimney of his house on fire Richard Scarr was fined Is. , THEFT.—Michael Roderick was charged with having stolen from the shop of James Bacun and Son, Sankey- st., a pair of child's boots, value 2.-s, on Friday, April 13th. He was also charged with having stolen from an unoccupied house in Palmyra-square, four keys, value 4s, on the same date. The boots were identified by Al- bert Pritchard, manager of the shop, and it was proved that prisoner attempted to pawn them, but not being able to give a satisfactory account of his possession of them they werq handed over to the police, and prisoner was taken into cuttody. It was afterwards discovered , that they had been taken from the shop of Messil: Bacup , and Son. Prisoner, who pleaded not guilty to the first charge, but guilty to the second, was sentenced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour in each case. .CANAL BOAT NinsascE.—William Deakin, Northwich, was summoned for allowing the Sat " Active " to remain in a defective condition, and James Bracegirdle, the mas- ter, was summoned for aiding and abetting. Inspector Norman said that he found the flat moored in the Mersey, and on examining it 'found it to be in a. very dirty and defective condition. Mr. Deakin said that the boat be- longed' to the executors of the late James Deakin, and he represented the owners. It was the fault of Bracegirdle that the Sat had not been repaired, and he had been fre- quently ordered to have the flat laid up forthat purpose. The magistrates fined Brake:irate lOs and costs, and the case against Deakin was dismissed. PlText AND Toss.—For playing this game in Mass- 116u.se-yard, on Good Friday, Walter Whitley was sent to, gaol for seven days. . Scnoor, ATTENDANCE CASES. The following cases brought forward bY Mr. Georoe Riley, on behalf of the , School Attendance Committee, were dealt with under the Education Art :—The son of Joseph Fillingham, forge- man, Dallam-lane, was ordered to be sent to the ship Clio " ; John Rooney. forgeman, Crossley-st., fined lOs ; John Ward, forgeman, Old-road, fined 55; Wil- , liara Hurst, wire-drawer, General-St., fined ss; Cilther. Me Clancy, Silver-square, fined ss; Thorna§ Water- worth, labourer, Old-road, fined 3s 6d; Michael Flynn, forgeman. Bewsey-road, fined ss; Michael Coffey, forgeman, Bank Quay, fined 58, A case agaiDst Joseph Whitlow, butcher, Fennel-ft.% *al dismissed, and the son of Thomas Maitinson, labourer, Bank-st., was or- dered to receive six strokeswith the birch rod. LICENSE TRANSFERS. The following transfers of licenses wert granted :—Green Dragon Vaults, from Martha liorrocks to John Naylor Horrocks ; Blyie Lion. from Joseph Sutton to George Lambert; Crown and Sceptre, Buttermarket-st., from John Williamson to Levi Allcock ; Golden Lion, Latchford, from William Whit- taker to John Williamson • and an off-license in Chorley- st., from Levi Allcock to Robert Savory. TUESDAY.—Before Alderman Pickmere and Councillor Francomb. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—For having been drunk and disorderly in Dial-st., on Monday night, and also for hav- ing assaulted Julia Quinn at the same time and place, John Illley was fined ss. including costs; David Hughes, for having been drunk in Buttermarket-at., on the same date, was fined 58 and costs. LICENSE GRANTED.—Temporary authority to sell beer to be consumed off the premises was granted to Thomas Garnett, 51, Lord Nelson-st. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley. SLEEPING OUT.—Michael Cloe, a labourer, was.brought up in custody on a charge of sleeping on the premises of Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co., Liverpool-road, on the previous night, and was sent to prison for seven days with hard labour. DRITNIEENNESS.--JOhR Cooney, last frchn Liverpool, a lahcarrer, was committed to prison for seven days, with hard labour, for been drunk in Mersey-street on the previous evening. TUCRSDAY.—Before Major Litton, Alderman Webster, and Councillor Greening.. ntEFT ET A LIMY BRICIELATER.—Thomas Wilson, a bricklayer, was charged with having stolen from a house in course of erection on Knutsforekroad, on Tuesday evening, two bricklayers' trowels, value 4s, the pro- perty of Samuel Brown, one of the workmen. Prisoner, who hails from Lymm, had been won near the house on . the evening on which the trowels were stolen, with a trowel in his possession, and a description of him was given to the police. •On Wednesday afternoon P.C. Monaghan was on duty at Market Gate, when he saw prisoner getting on a 'bus that was going to Latchford. Seeing that his appearance agreed with that of the man suspected of stealing the trowels, and noticing some lime on his boots, he questioned him, and as he gave different accounts of himself, took him into custody. On being searched, two pawn tickets, each relating to trowels, were found upon him.—Prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was sentenced to one month's imprisonment, with hard

labour. DRINK AND ViocExcE.--Emanuel Smith, who said he belonged to Sheffield., was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Filling's-court on Wednesday evening, and with assaulting Mary Connolly by kicking her at the same time and place. The magistrates, after. hearing the case inflicted a fine of fis and costs in the first case, and dismissed the charge of assault. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and 'Dr. Gorman. BEGOING.—John Platt, who was brought up for begging in Sankey-st, on the previous afternoon, was dismissed on promising not to offend again. DRUNKENNESS.—Thomas Hannon was charged ' with having been drunk in Parker-st. on the night previous. He was dismissed with a caution. ALLEGED WIFE DESERTION.—.Tames Hesford, black- smith, Oldham, was summoned for deserting his wife, who is living with her mother in James-St., Warrington. He expressed willingness to maintain his wife, but said that he could not afford more than es per week, which 'he had been paying for some time. The magistrates made an order upon him to pay that amount.
WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. Wanicasnay—Before Mr._ James /damn and Mr. W. H.

_ Bleckley. DRUNKENNESS. James Taylor, engine driver, em- ployed on the Ship Canal works, was fined 2s 6d and costs for having been drunk and disorderly at Rixton on the 29th ult, and a similar penalty was imposed upon John Hill Grundy for having beea drunk and disorderly. at Croft on the let ink. For a similar offencetcommitted at Warrington on the 14th met, was fined 5s and costs. A fine of as 6d and costs was imposed upon Patrick Garvin for having been drunk 4t Burtonwood on the 14th inst. OasTaccrioN.—Joserth Mounfield was fined 5s and coats for having caused an obstruction of the footpath in Manchester-road, by allowing a quintity of becks to remain there an unreasonable length of time.

LYIVIM PETTY SESSIONS. FRlDAY.—Before MesSrS. P. Stubs, T. P. Norris, and C. Lister. DRUNKENNESS.—Wm. Thomason, drunk and disorderly, at Lymm, on 24th March. as 6d and costs; Thos. Clare, drunk and disorderly, at Lymm, 25th March, 2s 64 and costs ; Thomas McTighe, drunk and disorderly, at Liirm 12th April, 2s 6d and-costs •, and Martin Burke, and disorderly, at Lymm, 24th March. 2.s 6d and costs. .CARELESS CARTERS.—George Eckersley, of Warring- ton, was fined 5s and costs for having been asleep in his cart on the night of the sth April, at Lymm; Michael ' Egan; for having driven a horse and cart without reins, atLyram, on the 17th April, was dismissed with a cau- tion. A Tascrioly ENGINE OFFENCE. James Barker, of Lymm, was charged with having driven a traction engine along the highway at Broomedge, between the hours of 7 p.m. and 3 a.m., contrary to the bye-laws, on the 27th March. In defence, it was stated that the engine had broken down on the Sway. A fine of 2s 64 and costs was imposed. ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—George Richardsdh, brewes, of Altrincham, was charged with having caused a horse to be worked at Lymm on the 16th March when in an unfit condition; and John Murray was. charged with having worked the horse while in an unfit state. Mr. Brown, of Stockport, defended. Evidence was given by P.C. Dutton, Inspector Aplin, and Mr. A. Monroe, veterinary surgeon, for the prosecution but the case was dismissed. Smoot ATTENDANCE CASES. Several parents were summoned for not having sent their children regularly to school, and in the case of Mr. John Jackson a fine of 5s was imposed. The other cases were either a:djourned or dismissed. SLEEPING IN AN OUTBITILDING.—A tall and rather respectable-looking young man, named Hugh Rogers, was charged with having slept in an outbuilding at Lyinm. The prisoner stafed that he had recently come from America., and had been without food for two days. Being tired and hungry he went into the outbuilding to sleep, not knowing that he was violating the law. He added that he was going along the canal to get work, having previously had a fortnight's employment. Ile was dismissed with a caution. Bnoopm.--James Carroll, charged with begging at Booth's Hill, Lymm, was sent to prison for sever days.
Mr. Snelling, an English Rome Rule delegate, was on Thursday sentenced by the County Court judge of Clare to two months' imprisonmentior inciting persons to join the National League. ,

played a yery good game, as alsq di the Runcorn mem- bers. Edcles made every attemilt to score, but failed to bring off anything important. At the call of "No side" the visitors were •leclared the victors, the score being, Runcorn, one goal and five minors, to Eccles two tries and four minors. Teams—Runcorn: J. Brazendale back; T. Davies, W. A. Riley, and R. Cookson, three- quarter backs; H. Hughes (captain) and G. Whitby, half-backs; J, Clarke, W. H. Broady, G. T. Wainwright, F. Hancock. W. Stubbs, R. Dolan, J. Gayter, P. Riley, and A. Hampson forwards. Eccles: J. Grundy, back; J. Worthington (Captain), F. Potter, and F. Halsall, three-quarter backs; J. Drury and G. Bridge, half- backs; F. Lunn, W. Chambers' E. Blakemore, C. Holt, B. flaslingdoz, J. Worthington, A. Rowbott,om, W. Davies, and T. Taylor, forwards.
WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER FREE WANDERERS.

This matcb was originally fixed to te played at Man- chester on Saturday, March 26th, but owing to the West Lancashire Cup Final Tie being played at Warrington on the same date, the " wirepullers " were unable to raise a team, cunstquently the match was postponed. Arrange- ments had been made in the meantime to change the venue, and Monday night last having been selected to bring 911 the contest, only a meagre attendance favoured the sport. Both teatila We Weak, and in enjoyable Weather the visitors started operations against it stiff breeze, and only a feeble reply being made, hostilities Were found to reign at neutral ground. The first to break the ice was Antro- bus, who passed neatly to Barnes, the latter handing his charge over to .folley&Veho placed the Wanderers on ' their defence. Ashtonrcharged Hindle's kick down, and Davies became prominent by a, neat dribble. Give-and- take play of an interesting nature followed, until Jolley relieved the monotony by a'grand run, which placed the, Wanderers' goal in jeopardy. Barnes made tracks for the Manchester line, but a wild pass lost what groundkad been gained. Povey was here applauded for smart work and after a pretty exhibition of passing by the home team, Massey made off at top speed, and grounded ever the line, but unfortunately he had placed his foot in touch. A drop at goal by Barnes registered a minor for Warrington. Massey replied to Erskine'%drop-out, and McLeod temporarily relieved the pressure, but a screw kick by Barnes again found Warrington on the aggres- sive. Turner made a desperate effort to score, and tak- ing the leather over, had the satisfaction of seeing Davies complete the try, no goal resulting from the place. Speakman and Ashton became prominent with neat work until Hindle checked them. After Anderton and Erskine had dribbled neatly, Barnes took the ball from their feet, and almost landed a goal. Speakman, Fair. Turner. Ash- ton, and Jolley passed to each other, and Holt was com- pelled to save. Barnes put in a dodgy run from the drop-out, and Ashton again placed the visiting team on the defensive. Antrokus passed smartly to Speakman, who dodged past . his opponents, and groun- ded over the line. Barnes took the place, and' registered the premier point. Jolley threatened danger soon after the re-start, and Barnes put in a use- ful run and pass to Antrobus. Molynemc saved a rush by Armstrong, and after Massey and Barnes had passed and repassed to each other, Jolley secur4d possession at half way, and threaded his way through the thick of his opponents, only to be tackled on the line by Holt. Half time was then called, the scpre standing at War- rington I. goal, 1 try, 3 minors, to nil. McLeod only made a faint reply to Turner's kick off, and before the visitors were aware et their situatioti Barnes dropped a goal. This last success of the home team seemed to have taken the visitors by surprise4et on the recommen4- ment Woods found an opening, and took the oval to the Warrington line. However, the visitors' stay was only of short duration, for Speakman and Fair. Turner took play to the Manchester line, and Holt was compelled to concede a minor. The drop out brought little relief to the visitors, for Fair Turner made a grand rush from the line out. Povey was conspicuous by sure tackling and smart dribbles, and after the last-named had been dis- appointed on sevesal occasions his efforts were re- warded by scoring after a neat dribble from the quarter ' flag. No goal resulted. Exchange kicks by Hindle and Massey ended in the latter following up his own kick and, securing possession, racing over the line. Barnes • kicked a goal. The Wanderers no played up, and after some desultory play they were enabled to score, and Hindle Made a good shot for the premier point. t Nothing of interest occurred now, and time was eiven- tua,lly called, the score reading,—Warrington, 3 goals, 6 2 tries, 8 minors; Free Wanderers, 1 try, 1 minor. 6 The game was a grandly contested one. The passing of the home backs was excellent, whilst the dribbling • and tackling of the forwards was Superb. The three- quarters have seldom been seen to greater advantage all • three playing with a combination that has rarely been seen on the Wilderspool enclosure. Nevins made but a L poor show at hack, whilst both Introbus and Speakman 6 passed and saved in first-class style. Povey was the best forward on the field, his efforts being seconded by Ashton and Turner. On behalf of Free Wanderers, Hin- dle, Erskine, and Anderton, were the pick. The following were the teams :—Warrington: W. Nevins, back; J. Jolley, T. Barnes (captain), and J. T. Massey, three-quarter backs; W. Speakman and Antro-• bus, half backs; H. Aekton, Fair. Turner W. Povey, R. Littlewood, W. Dillon, T. Davies, Thorrily, Isherwood, and Atolyneux, forwards. Wanderers: Holt, back; M'Le,od, Woods, and Hindle, three-quarter backs; Arm- strong and Muntoe, half hacks; Schofield, Thurmaia, Erskine, Walker Makinson, J. Anderton, Worthington, and two otkers:forwards. WARRINGTON V. KENDAL HORNETS.

In splendid weather the Warrington first team made the journey to Kendal on Saturday, to fulfil their return fixture with the leading club of the Lake District. The. Warringtonians were only indifferently represented, as the brothers Turner and Jolley were absentees; but, on the other hand, the Hornets mustered their "best pos- sible." A fair number of spectators witnessed the en- counter, and although the home team were confident of victory, the visitors played in resolute style, only being beaten by one try and five minors to one minor. Barnes was unfortunate in losing the toss, as a glaring sun and a slight breeze were against him, and Warring-. ton kicked off, Cross replying to half-way. From the first scrimmage formed the Hornets' forwards obtained possession, and took the leather over, Wilkinson scoring. Armstrong took the place, but failed to land the premier point. This sudden reverse, before the ga,me had thoroughly settled down, seemed to stagger the War- ringtomans, and from the drop-out they went bff with a dash that seemed as if they were going to equalise in the next minute. Speakman passed to Barnes, who dropped the oval into touch at the Kendal 25. Massey was to the fore with brilliant work, but Battersby saved his side at a critical juncture.' Speakman and Warren again placed the home side on the defensive,, and from a line out Davies passed smartly to Evans, who got to the line. The leather was taken over by Ashton and Povey, the visitors almwt scoring. Handles cleared his line soon after the drop out, but Baines and Ellwood forced Massey to -concede a minor. Evans intercepted a pass of '
THE •EXAMINER, SATYRDAY, APRIL 21, 1888

Walk' d pr4ssureAvas rought to hear on the.",in- gOV. However, Armstrong relieved: and a long' kick by Barnes was neutralised by the safe play of Allan. W. Dillon headed a dribble here, and his effort was aided by the pretty passing of Warren and Barnes, which se- cured a little headway. The Hornets' skipper came to the front with a smart run and punt to half-way, but a moment later Speakman saved a dangerous rush of the home team forwards. Give-and-take play now tOok place at neutral ground, until pretty exchange kicks by MaSsey, Evans,' and Allan found play at Kendal quarter flag. Battersby no* became conspicuous by clever work, and* the same player, through a misun- derstanding, was enabled to -relieve the pres- sure by a run to ,the Warrington quarter flag. The game was now vep, fast, and Parsons and Baines were conspicuous by good runs to the Warrington line. Mulling. by the home backs served as relief to the War- ringtornans, and Massey punted grandly to Allan, the latter replying to the visitors' quarter flag. Walker now made tracks for the visitors' goal, but found his equal in 'Massey. Battersby made his mark in a dangerous posi- tion, but the kick at goal proved futile, and only a minor was registered. Soon after the drop-out Donohue, Povey E. Dillon, and Ashton made an effort, only to be repulsed by Cross. W. Dillon rushed the oval to the Kendal line, and from a pack here Warren passed passed splendidly to Evans, who, with excellent judgment, transferred to Massey, the latter taking his drop at goal, but failed to raise the ball from the ground. Battersby now showed up, but half-time was called with the score at Kendal Hordets one try and three minors to Warrington one minor. The second half was commenced by Walker, Barnes replying. Exchange kicks by Walker, Baines, Battersbv, and Massey added no advantage .to either side, and after some desultory play Nimes spoiled Arm- strong when the latter threatened danger. Wilkinson now headed the Kendal forwards in a dribble/to the line, and Nevins saved his side from further disaster by touch- ing down. The, drop-out found pL'y at half-way, and Massey was awarded a free kick for a fair catch. The visitors now seemed determined, to score, and an effort by Speakman nearly had the desired effect. Free kicks were frequently indulged in by each side, and Warren and Evans by smart tactics took the game to the Kendal line. Some rough work was now, witnessed, and desper- ate efforts were made by Povey and Davies. Quick pas- sing by the home team relieved to the quarter flag, and Baines took the leather to half way. The Warringtonians now indulged in some neat passing, and Massey again became prominent by his sure tackling. Warren tried to effect an oPening here, but Cross prevented. The visi- ting team were now playing with great determination, and forced the Kenilal men to adopt the defensive, and although Armstrong temporarily invaded the Warring- ton quarter, Massey forced the game back to the North COuntrymen'slines. E Dillon and Ashton dribbled smartly, and Davies made a fair catch, punting to the, quarter flag. The game was now virtually over, and no sooner had the Warrington team begun to make tlieir final effort than the whistle called for "No. 5ide,".146.17- ing the Warringtonians the losers by one try, five minors to one minor.

The hothe team were undoubtedly lucky to win, but they took the first opening that presented itself, and be- fore the visitors were aware the game had been started the winning point was scored. Massey was the best back on the field. His tackling was superb, whilst Ais timely apd well-judged kicks quite nonplussed the Ken- dal teard and spectators. Evans made a creditable show at centre, but Barnes appeared out of place at wing three-quarter. Nevins only shone occasionally, whilst at half no choice could be, made in either Warren or Speakman. In the front rank Davies, Bandies, and Donohue deserve distinction. On behalf of Kendal Hor- nets, Walker. Cross, Baines, and Ellwoodgiere the pick: Anlincident which occurred during the sec&d half might be mentioned. Armstrong having been collared with the oval cried "Held" in the usual manner, but on being released he made off again •at top speed without ,1 any opposition being offered to his career. An appeal was lodged that the ball was dead, but the referee (Mr. Bland) allowpd the try. However, the Kendal captain (Mr. Walker) came to the rescue of the Warringtonians, and having overheard his man cry "Held," he sports- manlike, ordered his men to scrimmage the ball back at centre field; thus reversing the referee's decision. The following were the teams :—Warrington : Nevins, back; Massey, Evans, and Barnes (captain), three- quarter backs; Warren and Speakman, half-backs: Ash- ton, W. Dillon, E. Dillon, Davies, Bandies, Littlewood, Donohue, Fovey, and Hayes, forwards.' Kendal Hor- nets: Allan, back; Walker, Battersby, and Armstrong, three-quarter backs; W. pLAso ow EXHIBITION. - NOISSRS. CROSFIELD'S SOAP. _

The sup exhibit of Messrs. J. Crosfield and S which has just been completed at Glasgow, is a rem - able one, and, following that shown last year at Liv - pool, (a representation of which we give to-day) may be said to have inaugurated a new departure in the artistic and effective display of this many-colour production, as against the old style of never-varying obelisks which seemed to be the only orthodox form in which manufacturers bf soap dared exhibit their indis- pensible wares. A change has been wrought, and under the spell we are introduced to all the vividness of Oriental coloring. The soap. assuming the form of an Egyptian mosque, is designed with considerable breadth, and con- veys an impression of the strength of a citadel such as may be seen on the banks of the Nile. It consists of a principal octagonal tower rising with minarets to about 12 feet in height. There are two minor towers, square in form, with all the characteristic features of zig-zag mouldings, lozenge diapers, shaped crestings, and ribbed dome. A balcony connecting two parts of the edifice, and the inlaid pavement which surrounds the whole, are very happy in their rendering of Egyptian coloring, and ' will remind many a traveller of those striking and im- pressive piles in that ancient land. Without entering.in- , to ixtrticulare respecting the qualities of saap inchldeti in the exhibit, we may state that they 'comprise the leading sorts of household and toilet soaps sold in the home trade, besides the special manufactures for Jays, China, India, the Cape, west coast of Africa, South America, the West Indies, Canary Islands, aid others of less importance. Referring to the exhibit, at the Livetpool Exhibi- tion, as depicted above, the " Illustrated • London News" said, on November 13, 1886 :—Visitets to the Liverpool Exhibition this year have admired the tasteful, ingenious, and effective manner in which 'Messrs. Cros- field have displayed their products. The specimens of soap h ave been arranged as part of a beautiful architec- tural device of Oriental character, Byzantine in its general plan, with Samcenie features, and the design re- flects much credit on the originator. The most striking feature of the structure is its charming variety and blending of colour. Bases and wills are executed in complementary tints, while architrave, frieze, cornice, and other details of the entablature are picked out in delicately blended and contrasted hues, the wilble pre- senting a most inviting appearance considered merely as in artistic design. It is composed entirely, of soap, and mainly of different kinds of mottled soap, while the "Perfection Soap" is Used for the corner cupolas of the elegant temple. In the grounds of the Exhibition another attractive exhibit of this enterprising firm is to be seen near the Balloon and the Indian Village. Here has been erected a quaint and inviting kiosk, so painted as to sug- gest that it has been cut out of eblue mottled soap. It is 'attractively furnished in the interior; and, besides floral decorations, contains a beautiful display of toilet soaps, and of many-coloured mottled soaps, exquisite in tint and manufacture. The hangings and decorations of the kiosk are effective. • The walls and ceilings are draped in rich Oriental colours, and the roof spangled with stars. Considering Messrs. Crosfield's exhibit in its entirety, everyepe who sees it will acknowledge it to be one of the greatti* attractions of the Exhibition. Want of space prevents our giving a more minute description of these unparalleled exhibits, for which Messrs. Crosfield,have obtained two gold medals (the highest awards given at the LiverpoorExhibition), one for "Perfection Soap," the other for general excellence in manufacture of all soaps. Crosfields'Perfection Soap is offered as the out- come of long and Most expensive scientific experiments; for cleaning floors, paint, kitchen, and other rough ,household work, it cannot be excelled. Its greatest victory will be obtained in the laundry, where it will in- deed prove itself a "wonder worker." Its great lather- ing and dirt-extracting properties will lighten the toil of the user, make clothes cleaner and whiter, and save its own cost to the purchaser, for no soda or dry soap need be used with this wonderful washing soap. Against disease and infection it is all-powerful, being a pure dis- infectant, and, as a skin soap, it is invaluable.
