Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning

• RUGBY RULES. RUNCORN V. ECCLES "A" TEAMS.—On Saturday the Runcorn 'IA" played their last fixture of the season, on the Irwell-Tane enclosdre, and thrashed their opponents in a most decisive manner. The game was marred at times by a little ill-feeling, which, however, passed off. For Runcorn, Booth, Crompton, and Lunt were the pick. The forwards completely overplayed their opponents. Ebcles were best represented by Byers, Boothman, and Ellison. The final score was, Runcorn, 4 tries 10 minors to Eccles nil.

WIDNES ON TOUR.—On Friday night last the Widnes first team departed for a tour into Westmoreland, inten- ding to meet Kendal aria Barrow. The match with the first-named club took-place at Kendal on Saturday. Wil- son, the home captain, tnade two splendid runs in the first half of the game, which caused play to be hotly con- tested on the visitors' lines. A try gained by Winskill was strenuously objected to by Widnes, but the referee allowed the try. The place kick failed. A scrim- mage was formed at cen,tre. The second half was noisy, and scrambling play was the order of the day. Bell and Banks, for Kendal, kicked and ran well, as did Plumpton and Hardman for Widnes, who had the best of what play there was in this half. Widnes scored two minors qpi6kly and eventually got a try, whith the totin disputed, and the referee's decision being against aWidnes, the latter left the field ins body. The scoi, so far as is obtain- able, is a disputed try each. The second match was played at Barrow on Monday. From the kick-off Wid- nes were soon credited with a coliple of minors. Leake put in a kick which he followed up, and scored a try near touch, which was not improved upon. , Not long afterwards Widnes scored, a goal resulting. Barrow, al- though they were a man short, showed up vigorously, and Leake ran in beautifully, but ill-luck again attended their place-kicking, and they were ultimately beaten by a goal and two minors to two tries and two minors. RUNCORN V. ECCLES. Runcorn met the Eccles team on Saturday, on the ground of the latter, at Eccles, the visitors being minus W. Hughes and Faxilkner. Broady started the sphere for the Runeorn team at 3-30, before a meagre attendance, and Potter ston after gained a try for Eccles. Rowbottom took the place, but failed to put the leather Over the bar. W. Riley, however, soon &idol- ised. Brazendale took the place 'kick. and succeeded in gaining the premier point, and g half-time the visitors had scored one goal and one miner to their opponents one try and two minor. On change of ends, Lunn started the leather for the home team, and the visitors kept the play within the home 2.. for a length of time, after which Wainwright made a good attempt to drop a goal, but failed, the ball going dead. After some sharp play on both sides, 'Drury made a fast dribble dowil.touch, and kicked, and Lunn follpwing up. grounded the oval over the line. The same player took the place kick, but failed, making a very poor attempt. The kome team I
THE, SHIP CANAL 'WORKS,
AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT:
No. 14.—LYMM AND WARBI7RTON.

We have seen that when at Thelwall a bend in the Mersey intersects the intend ozl refute of the canal the difficulty is met by the hiiking of a new channel, which will keep the waters of file river separate from those of the canal. Whep, however, the Mersey in its sweep in the direction of Lymm and round by Statham again crosses the line of the canal, this expedient is not, to be resorted to. The river is apparently not to be diverted, but left to run in its present course and where the two water- ways—the natural and the artificial—meet and in- tersect, their waters will blend and intermix. This of course means that at these points the levels, of the canal and the river are, or will be made, similar. We find from the plans that where the canal cuts through the bed of the Mersey at Statham, the ,ordinary water level of the river is just a little below the intended level of the canal.. This being the case, it follows that the level of the river will have to be slightly raised in order that the canal may be kept at its proper depth, and it is accordingly within the power; of the Canal Company to raise or lower the level of the waters of the Mersey, the Bol- lin, and the Irwell, and of the cuts, canals, and brooks connected with these streams. For this purpose they may remove or alter any of the weirs, banks, &c., between Howley weir at Wallington and Hunt's Bank, in Manchester. It is further enacted; as a protection to Lord Winmarleigh, that "if by reason of the execution of any of the works by this Act authorised, the ordinary level of the river Mersey be raised the company shall, in so far as any Acts relating to the company so require, raise the , banks of the said river and its tributaries to a cor- responding extent." The part of Lancashire Which is enclosed within the level of the Mersey reaching up to Statham is known by the name of Rixton Leys, and across these Leys the canal will be fur- nished with embankments so that it may be enclosed on both sides with banks of ten or twelve feet high. It is laid down that that part of the Leys Which lie to the south of the canal, and which will be severed from the rest by the canal, is to be purchased froze the owner, Lord Winmarleigh, by the Canal Company, at a price tube agreed upon, or, in case of difference. at such prices as shall be settled by arbitration in the manner provided by the Lands Clauses Acts. There are several other provisions for the protection of Lord Winmarleigh in connection with the mak- ing of the canal at this part of its course. One of these is that no canal tolls or wharfage dues shall be demanded or taken for certain specitied material, to be used for the cultivation of the Eixton estate, which has been carried on the canal or river in any vessel belonging to or hired by Lord Winmarleigh or his tenants and workmen. Another provision s that Lord Winmarleigh shall be. entitled to a ferry or passage acioss the canal or river by boats for the use of himself, his tenants and workmen, at or the existing ferry near to Butchers' Field locks, or at such other point as shall be agreed upon between the owner and the company. This ferry is to be free from all tolls and other ,charges leviable by the company, who must also, if so desired, ' construct the necessary slopes and approaches to ' the ferry on each side of the canal or river. The ; approaches will, however, be, made at the cost of , Lord Winmarleigh, and the working of the ferry , will at all times be subject to the bye-laws of the , company for the regulation of private ferries. , Where the canal first cuts through, from the direc- tion of ThelwalY, the bed of-the Mersey into Rixton Leys, and where it again pierces, the- river in leav- ing the Lays its channel will be considerably deeper than that of the river at these points, and, in 'order • to have the requisite depth, the latter will he deepened, in the first case, some ten or fifteen feet, I, and in the second eight or ten- feet, the river on the eastern side ot the Leys being a few feet deeper, than,at Statham. After leaving Buxton Leys the canal again runs on Cheshire territo7, though only ; for d short distance, as it once more intersects the , Mersey at the point near to where the latter is , joined by the Bollin. Along this part of its course, , which is Lymm township, the %tended surface , of the canal will-be a few feet 'below the natural level of the ground, but still not so far below as to L allow of artificial embanking being altogether done without. After passing from Lymm township ' into Lancashire, the canal will begin to run—opposite ; Warburton and onwards parallel with, and in pretty close proximity to the present bed pf the Mersey. With regard to Warburton We find that Mr. R. E. Egerton Warburton, a landowner in the . locality, is provided with a right of pre-emption over all lands taken or purchased from him in the township lying to the south of the canal, which shall not be required by the Canal Company for , the purposes of the canal or its incidental works, • or to enable the Company to comply with the pur- poses of their Act. Nothing in the Act is to preju- dice or interfere with any existing rights of wharfage on land belonging to Mr. Warburton, and adjoining the Mersey in the twnship of Warbur- ton, so long as the river remains available for traf- fic always provided that these rights 'of the landowner be exercised in subjection to the bye- laws of the Company for the regulation of private wharves. Should the present bed of the Mersey in this locality, be filled up, the Canal Company are to proVide a wharf or landing place, at or near the bridge carrying the Rixtoh and • Warburton road

div.head: AVARRINGTON FIELD CLUE.
div.p: AVARRINGTON FIELD CLUE.

, . - . Cr:4er the auspices of this Club, an interesting and largely-attended exhibition meeting, was held in the Lecture-room at the Museum, on Saturday evening. It may he mentioned that this valuable local club has been in .existence about four years. It has for its object the mutual improvement of its members in the study of natural history, and par- ticularly, pf the botany, zoology, and geology of the district; special attention being directed to the following branches of work, nantely,the compilation of a Warrington-flora ; the collection of information relative to drift boulders; and the renewal and com- pletion, where reguired, of the corresponding collec- tions in the Warrington Museum. For the furthe,r- ance ot this work, field meetiegs are held during the summer. and evening meetings for the reading of papers, exhibition of objects, and discussions, during, the winter. Amongst those present at the success- ful melting on Saturday evening were the Mayor and Mayoress, Mrs. A. R. Sttton, Councillor and Mrs. Greening, and Miss Greening, Councillor' Mrs. and the Misses Monks, Councillors W. Pierpoint,H. Roberts, T. Jolley, Mr. and Mrs. F. W. Monks, Mr. and Mrs. Linnieus Greening, the Misses Greening, Dr. and the Misses White, 1 Dr. Starkey Smith, Dr. Joseph, Dr. Gornall, Dr. Sherratt, 1 Dr. Peacocke, Professor A. H. Young, F.R.C.S., Mr. J. C. Young, Rev. S. Wilkinson, Rev. M. Stevenson, Rev. R. Phillips, Rev. 0. Whalley, Mr. C. Chorley, Mr. J. Lee, Mr. and Mrs. George Woods, Mr. and Mrs. H. Bond, Mr. and Mrs. W. Owen, Mr. Thomas Tunstall, Mr. J. L. This. tall, Mr. H. D. Barks, Mr. J. Fairhurst, junr., and Mrs. Fairhurst, Mr. F. Dutton, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, Mr. and Mrs. Madeley, and Mr. W. H. Woodcock (hon. secre- tary of the club). The objects exhibited were very var- ious and interesting. They included Lepidoptera of the district—butterflies, moths, &c.; in cases—which had been collected by Messrs. T. Tunstall, T. Acton, J. Col- lins, J. A. Jackson; and Linmeus Greening. Two cases of British mosses named and beautifully mounted by Mr. James Cashvof Manchester, were to be seen, as was also a small collection of local specimens of birds eggs, ex- hibited by Messrs. George Ellison and C. R. Billups. A fine collection in twelve cases of British reptiles and Bat- rachians, belonging to Mr. L. Greening, was much in- spected and admired. In the cases were living specimens of the ring snake, the common lizard, the slow worm, the great warty newt, the Common newt, palinated rlf,wt, Jersey frog, common frog, French tree frog, common toad, natterjack toad, and large toad. Amongst Mr. Greening's contributions there were also several bottles of preserved snakes, lizards, newts, frogs, specimens d the spawn of frogs, Sm. The nest and eggs of the lap- wing were, exhibited by Mr. J. A. Jackson, while in the ' class for botany of the district there were several sheets of beautifully mounted specimens illustrating the order Umbelliferseprepared and exhibited by Mr. C. R. Billups. The Coleoptera of the district 'were represented by , several cases of local beetles, arranged and exhibited by Messrs. James F. Dutton and C. R. Billups. One of the most curious and interesting of the exhibits was found in two cases containing a splendid collection of various editions of Gilbert White's "Natural History of Sel- ' borne." These valuable books belonged to Dr. C. White, a great admirer as well as a namesake of the Hampshire elergynian. The subject of "Blood Relations," was illustratediby a number of charts, pre- pared by Mr. A. J. Jolley, while the Hessian fly—the dreaded insect of agriculturists,—and its immediate re- lations were illustrated by Mr. Belly Kendrick, who ex- hibited several cases of insects in various stages of growth, and charts displaying the plants attacked by the insect, and its modus operaiuh. Two othet notiteable ex- hibits werelound in the sample case sent by Mr. Made- ley to illustrate a scheme of museinn arrangements, and in the group of plants arranged. by Mr. E. Green, of Bank Park, tp display the dissimilitude in plant life. A considerablelaumber of handsometand powerful micros- copes were arranged on tables "under the charge of Messrs. F. W. Monks. E. Ward (Manchester), A. T. Gill- anders, James P. Dutton, and S. Parsonage, itinr., and throngh these magnifying instruments severs series of curious and interesting objects, including minite living specimens, could be inspected. In the course of the even- ing, suitable refreshments were served at a table in the room. The gathering was, as we have said, a successful one and passed off most agreably. •

The carriers and lurry owners of Manchester and the district lleld a meeting on Wednesday night, and adopted a petition to the House of Commons against Mr Goschen's proposal to-tax wheels and vehicles.

It is further stated that no canal tolls shall be-demanded for any similar material which may be carried on the canal or river in vessels belonging to or hired by Mr. Warburton or his tenants and servants. The road which at present leads from , the village of Warburton across tke, Mersey to Rixton will, on the Lancashire side of the river, be broker into by the canal, and will in the future be carriedlover the canal by a swing, bridge. TECHNICAL EDUCATION IN WAR- .IZINGTON.

On Tuesday afternoon a public meeting was held at the Town Hall, Warrington, in compliance with a numerotisly-signed requisition which had been presented to the Mayor, "to consider the proceed- ings of the National Association for the Promotion of Technical Education, and the .desirability of for- ming an Association in Warrington to co-operate therewith." His Worship the Mayor (Alderman Sutton) presided. and amongst those present were the Revs. S. Wilkinson, Morley Stevenson, and E. J. Willcocks ; Aldermen Webster find Harrison; Councillors T. Monks, Wm. Pierpoint, R. W. Fran- comb, Thomas Jolley, J. E. Wright, Shaw Green, 1 and H. Roberts; Messrs. W. Long, John White, John Roberts, W. D: Houghton, J. Walker, C. Made- ley, Charles Chorley, W. Parry, E. J. Guest, Wm. Sharp, D. W. Finney, Linnteus Greening, J. Lyon Whittle, F. .W. Mcinks, John Fairclough. Wm, Gowen, John Fairhurst, junr., and William • Diggle, The Moon said he was pleased to call the meeting, because he believed the subject of techrical education which they had met to discuss was one of yery great importance. During last session two bills were intro- duced by the Government, one for England and one for Scotland. The English Bill, which was withdrawn, gave power to the Corporation in a town like Warrington to establish and maintain a technical school out of the rates; but, without going further into, the details, it was quite plain it was a question deserving of their best attention, and he was glad that it was''being defi- nitely raised. _ . .

MC. MADELEY said it would be seen from the circular convening the meeting that it was expected Mr. A. H. D. Acland, M.P. (secretary of the National Association), would be with them that afternoon. He had had a long correspondence with him, .And that morning he had re- cdved a letter from Mr. Adand as follows :—" House of Commons, April 16th, 1888. Dear Sir,—Our association will be very glad if you should agree to-morrow to form a branch or a Corresponding Committee of our association. Our earnest desire is to get practical information and help from the chief industrial centres, especially at a time when legislation on technical education is promised. We have found that useful work has been done where branches have been founded, in bringing together and concentrating information from men of experience both in business and educational work. The importance of the whole question in its bearing on our industrial and i commercial position as a nation s not easily overrated, and it is encouraging to find that gradually we are wak- ing up and realizing this. lam very sorry that I cannot be with you, as I am obliged to be at the House of Com- mons. Mr. Llewellyn Smith will explain dur work and answer any questions.—Yours faithfully, A. H. D. 'Amex')." It was also stated in the circular that Lord Winmarleighbad signified his intention, all being' well, of being present, but he was sorry to say that that morn- ing Lord Winmarleigh had sent word to the effect that his health would not allow him to be present. Letters of apology for non-attendance had also been received froqi Messrs. J. G. McMinnies, John Rylands, H. Blackly, • C. Parr, J. drosileld, R. Pierpomt, Joseph Davies, S. Rigby, T. J. Down, F. A. Roberts, and Wm. •Reysnolds and Co.

Mr. H. LLEWELLIgi &writ, ,8.A., B.Sc. (assistant secre- tary of the National Association f6r the Promotion of Technical Education) then gave an account of what the association of which he is secretary was, why it was formed, what it had done, and what were its aims. He pointed out that technical education, in the sense in which the words were used in the title of the association, did not only refer to technical instruction in the strictest and narrowest sense, but also to those much wider re- forms in our system of elementary, secondary, and com- mercial education which were demanded alike by prac- tial men and by educationalists of all types. The iasso- elation had no political complexion, it had no cut and dried schemes of its own, and its objects wer9 manifold, including the rousing and stimulating of local effort. I (Applause.) • Councillor F. Mosits moved the following resolution : "That an ,Association be formed with the following objects, viz. :—(I) "To collect information respecting technical instruction. (2) to discuss the desirability of encouraging the provision of such instruction, with spe- cial regard to the needs and circumstances of the town of Warrington; and (3) to co-operate generally with the National Association for the Promotion of Technical Edu- cation." He confessed to a certain amount of pessimis- tic feeling in the matter, as some ten years ago he and a few others established what was practically, and what certainly .was intended to be, a technical school. He collected over £3OO that the school might have a fair start, and at that point he wished to state that they were much indebted to Mr. George Crosfield for the veg.. handsome gift of £lOO. (Applause.) The home of the school was not what they would have liked'it to be. It was, however, the best they could get, and he must say that, compared to the Mechanic's Institution, which he attended many years ago, it was a very great advance upon anything Warrington hill had before. Certainly Warrington never had a laboratory to slompare to the one that was established in the school. The school

was kept on for two or three years, in the hope that a thirst was being developed for knowledge, and that, after some nursing, students would be found to fill the school, to enable it to be carried on in a satisfaztbry manner. From the beginningo to the close the school never wanted a sovereign; and the reason it was closed was entirely owing to a want of interest on the part of the young men for whom it was intended. The close of the school VMS entirply

due to the lack of students, and not to the lack of means. He consented to the close of the school with a great deal of regret, and with a sort of feeling that as far as he was concerned he would never make another effort in the 1 same direction. He, however, now found himaelf enlisted in the same cause again. He would not enter into the desirability of technical education, which was a very wide one. They all had their own opinions about it. He had very decided opinions, and in his own way was carrying them out, so that whether the school was formed•or not, his firm would not be left high and dry. (Hear, hear.) • Mr. W. Low; seconded the motion, ,and thought the peoPle of Warrington had not commenced A moment too -soon to take the matter of technical education into con- sideration, if one was to believe all he heard. He thought that anything that would tend tc& disseminate informa- tion throughout the country on the points they admitted to be wanting must have a good effect upon the people generally. (Hear, hear.) Mr. JOHN Wurrn supported the resolution. _He was afraid they could not at present expect that they would have a technical, school in Warrington, but he appre- hended that they might anticipate something of the sort as the result of that meeting, and that they might, in the meantime, attain the same ,end only in a smaller way. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Mundella some time ago said he was perfectly,agh.ast and astounded at the progress which technical 'education was making abroad, and it was certainly a matter of regret that at a time when foreign competition was increasing so much we shouldbe so far behind in that particular. In Germany, he be- lieved it was, or used to be, the practice to have the/ apprentices ,pass an examination before their indentures were returned to them. He thought that was a very good plan, and it would be well if something of the kind could be tried in this country. He himself was connected , with agriculture more then any othtr trade, and he must give expression to his great desire that some steps should be taken whereby agricultUrists might become better acquainted with the pursuit in which theywere engaged. They saw farmers who were, generation after genera- don, farming in precis* the same way that their forefathers did, entirely ignorant of the` constitution of the soil they were tilling, or the crops they raised, or the manure they used; and although much had been done by means of agricultural societies and colleges to spread a knowledge of the subject, it was a Mere drop in the Ocean, and he as sure they would agree with him that some steps needed to be taken if that great industry: was to be perpetuated. (Applause.) Mr. Joniq FAnictotron said that, as President of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, it gave him great pleasure to support the resolution. The members of the Chamber were very , much in favout of technical eclue.a- don, and would help the movement in any vraythey could. (Applause.) The resolution was theictput to the meeting, and carried unanimously. Mr. E. J. GrrEsi proposed that Lard Winmarteigh be elected president of the local association, remarking that his lordship was much interested in the subject. The Rev. E. J. Vi'n,Lcocas seconded the resolution, and observed that, speaking for himself as being prac- tically engaged in the work of education, he could only say that he had come there that afternoon to receive in- formation on the subject, and that information he had received from the instruetive speech of Mr. Smith. The resolution was unanimously passed. _

- • Coun. T. JOLEEY proposed "That Messrs. F. Monks J. White, F. A. Roberts, and C. Madeley be appointed a provisional committee to receive the names of members, and to arrange for the first meeting of the association." lie was sure, he said, that the project would receive the supoort of the inhabitants of Warrington.. Mr. WILLIAM OWEN briefly seconded the proposition. Mr. CORNEY, speaking as th 6 representative of the elementary school teachers of Warriugton, supported the proposition mei expressed the pleasure that the elemen- tary schooeteachers felt at the prospect of an associa- tion being formed. Be hoped that some inquit7 would

be made into' the system Of education in elemental schools. In Warrington pupil teachers were eitgaged 1 that avocation during the whole of the day, and had fl time to pursue thnir own studies. They, as teachers, desired certain reforms that'therbelieved would tend 4 the removal a the irlts existing. In his opinioni added,, they were ma ufacturing in schools, not skill'y workmen, but clerks. 'There was a tendency aro% lads trained in elementary schools to lo& down up% trade, and to seek positions as clerks. He hoped that tpl Committee would inquire into the educational needs ° the town as regarded eitmentary schools. The resolution was then carried. ' Mr. W. D. Hotroirron proposed a vote of thanks to Smith.for his address. He remarked that there was IL. doubethat the spread of -technical education would 75 for the good of the.country. The question for them --hoW far would ,it affect the manufacturers of W Hinton. Instruction in chemistry or drawing was" good thing, and a very desirable thing, but still the (tu tion for them was how far it would afect the inanofa,,s tures of their town. The present state *of trade such that a very small margin of profit was left to ufacturers and mechanical appliances of all kinds •_,r to be introduced in order to secure to the manufactio:`, anything like a margin of profit. Consequently lab°'!; generally had beCome so sub-divided that the labow. itself had become mechanical. Drawing might be n excellent thing for some trades, but the men who 17- most success in the manufacture of wire were these depended most on dexterity of hand. Mr. R. W. FRANCOMB seconded the resolution. said that it was intended toteachchijldreuot only ' but practice as well. He believed that in some I agriculture was taught, even among the small ct and such a method must have an excellent effect. workmen could practise in technical schools they much better be ableto hold their own against competition.

ItY object in writing is twofold- -to express my gratitude for a great 4 benefit, and to tell a short story which cannot fail to interest the feelings of many others. It is all about myself; but I have remarked tilat when a man tells the honest truth about himself he is all the more likely be of use to his fellow-creatures. ,To begin, then, you must know I had '°llg been more or less subject to attacks of bronchitis, a complaint that you axe aware is very common and troublesome in Great Britain in certain sea-, oiris of the year. Some months ago I had a very severe turn of it, worse, -I &think, than I had ever had before. It was probably brought on by my catch- 'llg cold, as we are all apt to do when we least expect it. Weeks passed by, aald my trouble proved to be very obstinate. It would not yield to medicine, 144c1 as I also began to have violent racking pains in my limbs and back, I L'ecame greatly alarmed. I could neither eat or sleep. If I had been a feeble, icilly man, i should have thought less strangely of it; but as, on the con - ,4ary, I was hearty and robust, I feared some new and terrible thing had got liold of me, which might make all my strength of no avail against it. I say, tlat was the way I thought.

Presently I could not even lie down for the pain all over my body. I asked 4,1 Y doctor what he thought of my condition, and he frankly said, "I am sorry to have to tell you that you are getting worse!" This so frightened my fliends, as well as myself, that they said, " Thomas, you must yo to the hospital; it may 'e your only chance for life!"

I3ut I didn't want to go to the hospital. Who does P when he thinks he a,ll possibly get along without doing it. I am a labouring man, with a large kinily depending on me for support, and I might almost as well be in my

• 4. l 3 •4 grave as to be laid on my back in a hospital unable to lift a hand for inonths, Lor God only knows how long. Right at this point I had a thought flash across my mind like a streak of sunshine in a cloudy day. I had heard and read a good deal about Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and I resolved, be- fore consenting to be taken to the hospital,. I would try that well-known

remedy. On this I gave up the doctor's medicine and began taking the Syrup, Mark the wonderful result! I had taken but three doses within twenty-four hours when I was seized with a fit of coughing and threw up the phlegm and mucus off my chest by the mouthful. The Syrup had loosened and broken it up. Continuing with the Syrup, the racking pain, which I believe came from the bitter and poison humours in my blood and joints, soon left me entirely, and I felt like going to sleep, and I did sleep sound and quiet. Then I felt hungry, with a natural appetite, and as I ate I soon got strong and well. I felt I could leap through the air with delight!

In a week I was able to go to my work again. It doesn't seem possible, yet it is true, and the neighbours know it. There are plenty of witnesses to prove it. And, therefore, when I say I preach the good news of the great power of Seigel's Syrup to cure pain and dispase. far and wide, nobody will wonder at me.

div.head: OUR LONDON LEITER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LEITER.

LONDON'. THURSDAY NIGHT. Within the past week trouble has suddenly de- veloped in two important centres of the continent. The Emperor of Germany is evidently passing away, and General Boulanger is as certainly coming to the front. This time last week the Emperor was ap- parently in a condition that enabled the writers of the bulletins to invest them with an air of sanguine expectation.- Then aggravated symptoms, attribu- ted by the doctors first to inflammation, then to blood poisoning, developed, and, according to the latest news, the end is not far off. Ever since the Emperor, • then Crown Prince, rode throegh the streets of London, the stateliest figure in the Jubi- lee cavalcade, he has been a popular favourite here. But if there had been in the public eye no pleasing reminiscence of his soldierlike bearing, his heroic conduct throughout his illness would successfully appeal to sympathy and admiration. In these days, when Kings and Queens and Royal Prince& are too often either cruel tyrants, pettifogging money-grub- bers, or insatiable votaries of pleasure, it is some- thing of inestimable value for the vested interests of royalty, that among its ranks there should be one heroic figure. Whilst Germany is anxiously waiting by the bed- side of the Emperor with forebodings of what may happen when he is no more, France is hysterically helping on the new adventurer who is following with significant absence of originality in the foot- steps of Louis Napoleon. It is difficult for honest English people, judging only from theirown feel- ings and their national associations, to understand the possibility of Boulanger standing to-day in the formidable position he holds in France. The near- est parallel that nould be supplied by this country is to imagine the case of our 'Only General" up- setting the government of Lord Salisbury or Mr. Gladstone, and appearing as Dictator in the House of Commons. This vision is not possible for the average British mind, and even if for its purposes ' there were rolled together Lord Wolseley and Lord Randolph Churchill. But in France it is easy enough, as history has shewn since the end of last century, when the First Napoleon rose from his lieutenancy in the Artillery to be Frst Consul. What foolishness France pleases to perform in the national restlessness with authority is no busi- ness of ours. But, unhappily, the influence of General Boulanger, supposing he reaches the object of his now scarcely veiled ambition, will not be confined within the limits of the Departments of France. Boulanger is a symbol after the kind created by the First Napoleon. "C'est Boulanger gu'il noes fact" the Parisians sing. What they might more accurately shout is "C'est la revanche gu'il noes fact." Boulanger is the outward and visible sign of the inward and devilish hatred of Germany, which fills every French breast. Every- one feels that should he be carried into the Presiden- tial chair on the crest of a tumultuous popular wave he will be pledged to attempt to restore Alsace and Lorraine. That is a state of things that would have been bad enough even with the wise, peace- ful, and cool-headed Emperor Frederick on the Throne at Berlin. But with his place taken by the Junker Prince William the outlook would be troublous indeed. The House of Commons is approaching the con- clusion of the debate on the second reading of the Local Government Bill. This time last week Mr. Smith had not finally abandoned his expectition that the debate might be closed last Friday. When conviction was forced upon him, he hoped that an extension to Tuesday in this week would meet all reasonable demands, still reserving to-day for the Budget. But it was apparent that he had grown into the habit of fatally presuming on the good- will of the Opposition, and he Wtl4 g9Rirl!e4 to treat the debate more in accordance with pre- cedents that rule the second reading of first-class measures. The reader of the Parliamentary (letuatee will pro- bably have marvelled to note th ^ ' t whilst he the re' question in connection wi.' - Hill is the imposition the Local qevernment reference has be • the .Vith Via wheel tax, no tended deb.- made to ths subject in the ex- of the - _Actk on the seCond reading. That is one r tvisultS of the complexity of the whole bitsi- ..en. The tact is, that in Mr? Ritchie's Bill no re- letence is Made to the wheel tax or any other im- 'post designed to raise money by which the scheme i may be worked. These are n the province of the 'ttancellor of the Exchequer, and even as far as he is concerned do not come within the four corners of the 'lmperial Budget scheme. They have a bill all to' themselves, and it is ppon this that, by and bye, the gathering cloud of unpopularity raised by the Builget scheme will burst. Thanks to the spirit of fair play on the part of the Opposition, which is the striking novelty of the present session, extraordinary progress has been made with public business. But the programme put forward by the Government simply in respect of the Local Government Bill and the financial measures consequent upon it is in itself so stupendous that there is little hope of including any other important measure in the accomplished work of the session. The death of Mr. Matthew Arnold has created a profound sensation in London, where he was widely known. Me was not met in society so often as Mr. Kinglake, certainly not so frequently as Mr. Browning, who is one of the most accustomed guests and dullest companions met over a wide range of dinner tables. But Mr. Matthew Arnold went out a good deal, and, in company that he liked, Iva delightful. This was, however, only one of his moods, for he was a man capable of instinctive dis- likes, and there were some people whose presence acted upon him like a wet blanket. It WU all a thence, not to be determined before dinner. But to those permitted to enjoy intimacy of acquaintance, Mr. Arnold was bubbling over with fun. He had. a curious way of telling little stories against himself. There was one, published yesterday, which I have heard variously rendered. Mr. Arnold was talking about Mrs. Arnold, and said, " Ali, you should know my wife. She has all my charm of manner, and none of my conceit." Another story, which I have not seen in print, re- lates to the episode of his unsatisfactory visit as a lecturer to the United States, a work undertaken at great personal sacrifice, in order to meet what he regarded as a duty to his family. When the pro- ject was mooted tb him, Mr. Arnold urged that it was not hopeful, since he was very little known in the United States. "I do not suppose" he said, half ,hoping for contradiction, "that there are a hundred men in the United States who possess one of my books.' "Sirr, said the agent, "I assure you you are mistaken. I know America, and I will undertake to say that there is npt a small town or village that does not possess in its institute lib- rary a copy of "The Light of fAsia." That great work. little boys gone back to school from the Eas- ter holidays will know is the magnum opus of quite another Arnold- he who wrote in Tuesday's "Pall Mall Gazette" that verse to the dead poet "who bore my name," at which London is still sadly smiling: For Matthew Arnold to be known to pos- terity as bearing the name of the editor of the "Daily Telegraph is really too funny. Perhaps the most interesting event of the season, partly because it will be the most surprising, will be the production a Mr. Ilerkomer's'" Sorceress" at Bushey. I have not heard the mimic, and indeed the first rehearsal wa.s only last night, but the 'nisi en sine will perhaps be an event in the history of the theatre. Such illusion and so beautiful an effect I have never seen. It is as if nature were framed. There is a night scene in a wood, gipsies and their queen, and the stealing of a child. The trees stand out as natural trees, and not as painted cardboard; the moon moves in the heavens through fleecy clouds, and wanes at the approach of day; the cold dawn comes on, gradually the sky reddens, and shoots the Arm sunshine over the whole landscape. Mr. Herkomer has attained his results by his own

method, and they are miles away from ordinary scenic effect and within measurable distance of Nature herself. The theatre is a perfect little4mlld- ing, with wood carving as its only decoration, no patnt or stuoco, nothing but what time will mellow and improve. There are to be a series of perform- ances, one day for actors, one for artists, and so on. Mr. Irving is to come, Mr. Tree, Mr. Toole, the Ken- dells, and Mr. Hare. ,The thing has been kept an almost complete secret, and will have all the charm of surprise. The first performance will be next Tuesday. It is well known that anyone net better or more richly employed can edit a newspaper. To this widely-extended class it may be interesting to men- tion the fact that there is at the present moment a really desirable editorial chair going about begging for a suitable incumbent. It is situated in the office of " Freemans Journal." at Dublin. Since the death of Mr. Dwyer Gray the directors of the company which now possesses the property, have been on the look out for a worthy successor, and have not suc- ceeded in finding him. A man admirably-twited for the post, alike in respect of literary position, pro- fessional experience, and national sympathy. is Mr. Justin McCarthy, and I believe that, without any official step being taken, it has been bade known to Mr. McCarthy that if he were to put in an appli- cation for the post he would stand a pretty certain chance of being accepted. The appointment is worth haring, the salary being £2.000 a year. and the position on* of high personal dignity and in- fluence. But Mr. McCarthy has no uncontrollable hankering after the post, and has, I have reason to believe, resolved not to take the hint that has been dropped for his consideration. A paragraph has recently gone the rounds setting forth in detail the expenses of warming, lighting, and ventilating the Howie of Commons. It seemed a big sum, including p sum of £2,000 for , oil lamps. But the care and expense bestowed upon the com- fort of an English member of Parliament are nothing 'compared with those which the primitive sim- plicity of the Republic insures for United States Congressmen. I wonder what a member of the House of Commons would think if he suddenly dis- covered that by getting into a lift, and touching.an electric bell, he coul.i be conveyed to a palatial region, where the luxury of bhths, unequalled since 'the days of Pompeii, were at his lordly disposal. Such a state of things exists in the Capitol a'.; Wash - ington. There are all kinds of baths, hot, cold, tepid, and a Russian steam bath. Congressmen put down their names for a bath, as in the House of Commons members put down their names for tickets for the Ladies' Gallery, and their turn comes round with greater regularity.

div.head: 7atters to tbez. Obitor. A JUDGE OF POETRY!
div.p: 7atters to tbez. Obitor. A JUDGE OF POETRY!

Sir,—When an individual is ;with a burning vaulty to appear in print, you naturally expect him to " know something," to have read—if ever so little—and to have improved his mind above all pettifogging bias ; to have cured himself of all absurd " fads," and to argue his case—not to falsify his opponents' words, but to give them the meaning of their author. Now this is exactly what " Cadmus " can't do. His schooling has been too narrow—so narrow that he calls Thomas Hood a minor poet, and his verses "literary garbage !" "Cadmus" is a second "Daniel come to judgment," and deserves the proverbial putty medal! It is simply—may I say ? " throwing pearls to swine" (even at the risk of having that called literary garbage," too) to argue with such a rudimentary scribe, whose teetotal "fads" and literary vanity are on a par with his Paul Pry virtue—the (" as- sumed" only) right to meddle in other folks' concerns. And this is his religious notion of "doing as he would be done by!" Thank Providence, it is not mine. BELLEROPHON. Warrington, 19", 4, 1888..

THE RECENT LICENSING PROSECUTION. Sir, —I hope you will find space in your columns for a few remarks upon what may be called the extraordinary decision of the magistrates in the licensing prosecution on Monday week. The facts of the ..case were very simple. A woman, on coming out of a public house on Sunday monain*, is stopped bra, police officer and on being questioned as to whether she has any liquor about her stoutly denies that she has, but upon hearing that she will be searched, a large bottle is produced, which she says she has every right to take, as it is het hus- band's allowasce, the husband being the landlady's son. But if she knew that she was doing nothing wrong, and that she had every right to the liquor, why was it con- cealed? It is afterwards suggested that the defendant did not like to carry a bottle of beer ia the street on Sanday morning and so slipped it into her pocket. But ,a're ladies' pockets usually madetoaccommodate bottles a foot long and six inches wide? And even if this little discrepancy is accounted for,—if the bottle had been placed there for that reason, why did the defendant deny possession of it to the police officer? and why were her , relatives so anxious to see that the coast should be clear? Questions like these were hardly answered to anyone's satisfaction. Mr. Percy Davies did not think it right that tlo amount of reliance to be placed On the word of a witness should be determined by his character. As Mr. Davies said, "Re might tell the truth by accident." But the magistrates calmly accept the tale and dismiss the case. Is there not " Daniel " wanted in Warring- ton ?—Your's truly,

THE ROYAL SOCIETY OF LITERATURE. 1 Sir,—ln reply to the challenge contained in ydltir im- pression of the 10th ult., which should have been r. ponded to earlier, had I not been away from LOndon, I be to say that the elltßtlee fee and subs;Aption to this society are ontirelv a "post hoc" and not a" prop- ter hoc" of election, and to read the statutes otherwise is to read them wrongly. As regards a proof of my statement that "the fact of having produced some liter- ary work or the possession of some degree or diploma" is requ;red for election, I can only say that such is our rule and practice, whether the same be provided by the statutes or not. There must, as you are well aware, be exceptions to every rule. They are commonly said in- deed only to prove it, and in a Royal Society, munifi- cently aided by successive sovereigns of this realm out of their privy purse, it is scarcely too much to admit mem- bers of the Royal Family ipso facto and without further testimony! The late Duke of Albany, our lamented pre- sident for nine years, was at least an eminent example of Royal fitness for Fellowship. That we have not the gentlemen you enumerate amongst our Fellows is, I am bold to say, their loss as well as ours, and is certainly a neglect on their part of an obligation they owe both to them. selves and to literature. I am far, however, from accept- ing some of them as representatives of the highest stan- dard of English authorship except in a degenerate sense. Indifferent poetry and incorrect, and not seldom unintelligible English, too often disfigure their pages—so much indeed, as frequently to require what a recent writer Called intellectual pick-axes, to discover their meaning—and not one of them is worthy to hold a can- dle, I will not say to Shakespeare and Million, but even to Dryden and Pope, to Byron or Walter Scott. Simply adding tha,t the last-named great author was a medallist of this socibty, and asking you to remember that this is not essentially a society of literary men, but a society incorporated by Charter for the advancement of litera- ture—to effect which advancement properly, as you well know, the sinews of war are needed no less than the pos- session of learning.—l am, sir, yours obediently, E. GILBERT HIGHTON, M.A.

Cantab et Oxon, Barrister-at-Law, F.R.S.L., and Secretary to the Royal Society of Literature. [Mr. Highton has changed his ground. When asked, shortly after Mr. R. A. Nayloes election, to state wbat qualifications were necessary to become a Fellow

of the Royal Society of Literature, he said under date of -February 18th, 1888 :-110' The most satisfactbry reply I can give to your note of inquiry about the regulations for admission to Fellowship in this Society is to send you a copy of the charter and statutes, at

page r 8 of which you will find the information you ask for." We turned to page 18 and searched the regulations as directed, with the result, as previously stated, that we found not a word about literature, or literary work, or diploma. The essential qualification is, we repeat, an entrance fee of Three Guineas, and an annual subscription of not less. than "Two Guineas, to be paid in advance." Mr Highton would now have us put faith in some "rule and practice" of. which he furnishes no proof, and which is not provided for in the printed regulations to which he originally referred IS. But it won't do; the Royal Society _if Literature is (not for the first time) weighed in the balances and found wanting. Fancy Mr. R. A. Naylor having been accepted as a Fellow because of his intellectual appearance upon the great stage of the world." Can it be that the secretary. wlaen he wrote this, was poking fun at the new member who quotes Job wrongly, and wrongly ascribes the quotation to Shake- spere ? We admit, however, that Mr. Highton is a good secretary; he knows how to rake in the subscrip- tions—" paid in advance." But he ought to be candid, and admit that fora person to become a Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature does not necessarily mean that he has become a literary: fellow It is, we grant, a loss to the society that eminent literary men give it the cold shoulder—it is the loss of a large number of subscriptions. But "something too much of this." It would be wasteful to devote further space to the Society.—ED. Ex.]

THE MANCHESTER SHIP 'CANAL. (Continuedfrom page i) RUNCORN.

The work of excavating- is being briskly carried on in this section; in fact this is the only work that is being done at present. Four steam navvies and three Priest- man's grabs are in full operation, and they are making a lasting impression in the soil. From the big field to- wards Runcorn, a -broad channel nearly a mile in length has been made, and near the works of. Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele an excavation has been made. At this spot two "trial \holes are now being cut into the ground with the object of ascertaining the nature of the substance that will have to be encountered below the upper crust. So far only a beautiful red sand and . red clay have been met with, but, as the cutting here will reach a depth of 70 feet, it is highly probably that a rocky formation will have to be dislodged before the canal is completed. The spoil bank at Norton is assum- ing huge proportions. Day after day train loads of clay and other earthy matexial are driven in' rapid succession overthe bridge erected by Messrs Kirkham and Co., and deposited upon the Marsh. To the unprofessional eye this particular branch of the work would appear to re- quire little special knowledge, but it is, nevertheless, at- tended with its difficulties and its dangers. For instance, since the formation of the spoil bank was commenced, the ground upon which it was laid has sunk, on an aver- age, four feet per day, and a short time ago it sunk nine feet in one night. But, in consequenc:, of the spongy nature of the marsh, a depression at one point has caused a corresponding upheaval at another point not far dis- tant, and herein has lain the difficulty that has had.to be overcome, in laying the bank with safety, and accord- ing to the requirements of the case. The engineering skill of Mr. Gregson, the agent, has prevailed, and; as previously stated, the operations have proceeded without cessation.

M 0 0 RE. During the past week work has gone on with undimin- ished vigour in the neighbourhood of Moore, but there is nothing of more than usual interest to record. It may be mentioned that work has been in progress on this sec- tion for some four moths, and that about 800 navvies are at work, either in the cutting or preparing for the more destructive efforts of their powerful competitor the steam navvy. Within the large trench that has been cut at Acton Grange are several railway lines, laid 20 feet below the ground level, on which waggons and loco- motives are tonstantly moving about. On the far side of the channel there is a pumping station, draining hav- ing of late been found necessary. Here, for nearly half a mile, the huge basin has been cut out in its full width, though'not, of cottrae, to its entire depth, and from it a good idea can be e,rained of what the Ship Canal channel will look •like when it is finished. The engineering difficulties which have to be encoun- tered in the construction of the Ship Canal are well illus- trated in this neighbourhood. Following its straight course the canal cuts clean through two neighbounng and parallel railway lines, one of them the North-Wes- tern and the other a junction line. Before the railways are touched and .the traffic interfered with the Ship Canal Company will themselves have to make lines of divergence. In the end two railway bridges will cross the canal at a sufficient height to allow the passage of vessels. Another important matter is the diversion of the Mersey and of the turnpike road. Below Warring- ton the Mersey takes a bold semicircular sweep, and the road obediently follows its course. What the Ship Canal Companjr arel going to do is entirely to cut off the river loop of several miles, and instead to give the channel a direct course. In the same way the present turnpike road will cease to exist. It will be carried straight to Warrington across Arpley Meadows; the distance being 'more than halved. The road will necessarily cross the canal, and, as the traffic is not great the scheme of the company is not to erect a high-level bridge, but an easily-worked swingbridge. As the vessels come up the bridge will swing round. The whole thing will be the work of a minute or two, and no practical inconvenience will be caused. •

every instance almost were unrecognizable. Most of the poor fellows pi :sented the spectacle of a huge burnt cinder. Dr. Ormrod and Dr. Dudgeon, the works doctors, superintended the removal of the dead, and administered to the relief of those who were injured and dying.- At two o'clock in the morning the afterdamp became exceedingly stifling, and much against their inclination, the relief party had to stop work, owing to the unbreathable state of the atmosphere. The fire still raged in the pit, where the bulk of the men had been at work. At this time there still remained seventeen Men in the pit, who could not be approached, No doubt they had been dead for annin hours. It was now decided to fill the pit with water, with the object of putting out the fire. The news rapidly spread to all the vil- lages in the neighbourhood, where the majority of the workmen reside, and the arrival of the friends and relatives of the unfortunate victims, asking for tidings, which only increased thar grief. was a heartrending sight. On Friday morning the dead ' bodies were removed to the joiners' shop for identi- cation.

During the afternoon Mr. Willis received the fol- lowing telegram from the Home Office : —To Willis, H.M. Inspector of Mines, St. Helen's'Colliery, Work- ington.—ln reply to your telegram relative to St. Helen's Colliery explosion, I am to express Secre- tary of State's deep regret at calamity, and to say he is anxious to hear further particulars as soon as possible. INQUEST. . . . _

At three o'clock on Priday afternoon Mr. Wilkin Lunt, coroner for West Cumberland, opened an in- quiry at the Board-room of the St. Helen's Colliery Co. One or two of the relatives and several work- men gat e evidence as to the identification of the bodies. Mr. J. Holliday Johnson, certificated mana- ger of the colliery, was called, and in reply to the coroner and Mr. Willis, Government Inspector for the district, he detailed how the calamity hid hap- pened, bearing out telegrams already published. Mr. Willis said the men in the pit could not possibly be recovered, nor could the mine safely be entered in less than three weeks or a month. The inquest was therektpon adjourned to May 15th.

• WIDNES AMATEUR DRAMATIC SOCIETY. The third annual representation of the Widnes Amateur Elocutionary and Dramatic Society was given in the Alexandra Theatre, on Thursday even- ing. The success achieved by the society in former years ne doubt emboldened the members to produce Mi. E. J. Lancaster's amusing comedy "The Guv'nor," and in no spirit of flattery it may be said that most of the characters were portrayed in a manner th‘t would not have disgraced a first-class professional company. The merit of the perfor- 'mance was fully recognised by, the audience, and the only regret is that the accommodation of the theatre was much too ample for the number of per- sons praent. The following was the caste:— Mr. Butterscotch, a retired Confectioner... Mr. Richard Lewis Freddy, his son Mr. Harry W. Cookson Theodore Macclesfield, Boat Builder, Putney...Mr. G. E. Sayoe Theodore, his son Mr. J. Walwyn White -jellicoe, a retired Pickle Manufacturer...... Mr. W. E. Oakden Gregory Mr. Fred. W. Wareing The Mac Toddy, a Scotch Traveller Mr. Arthur G. Davies Cab Driver No. 3,407 Mr. T. C. Welding Mr. Vellum, a Lawyer Mr. Herbert White Ullage, servant to Itir. Butterscotch Mr. S. G. Webb Aurelia, second wife of Mr. Butterscotch—Miss E. A. Sampson Kate, Mr. Butterscotch's daughter by first marriage, Miss A. C. Davies Mrs. Macclesfield, wife to Old Macclesfield,

Mrs. Richard Lewis Carrie, their daughter, in love with Freddy Butterscotch, Miss A. M. Oakden The get up of Mr. Sayce, as the boatbuilder, was capital, and his acting of the part in all its broad humour was beyond criticism. Mr. Lewis's pour- 'trayal of the troubles of a jealous husband was highly diverting,, while as his stammering son Freddy, Mr. Cookson was in his element, and gave a capital exposition of a very difficult part. Mr. J. Welwyn White was quite equal to the task set him. The facial contortions of Mr. Wareing in his charac- ter of the " Tyke " were highly amusing, and Mr. bakden sustained well the tharacter of a sarcastic tormentor. Mr. Davies had a wonderful get up as Mac Toddy, but he was scarcely equal to the twang of the "bras,' Scottie." Each of the ladies fulfilled their parts with great credit, and Mrs. Lewis and Miss Sampson, who had the most to do, were especially noticeable. At the conclusion the whole of the performers were called before the curtain, and from the box of the president (Mr. T. H. Gossage) bouquets were thrown to Mrs., Lewis and Miss Sampson. Tile duties of stage manager were ful- filled by Mr. E. M. Davies, while Mr. Harry Cook- /son was an efficient acting manager; Mr. Howard C. Saire is the secretary of the society, and Mr. R. Lewis the hon. treasurer. The performance was re- peated to a good audience last night.

The owners of house property in Lymm have already felt beneficial effects from the commencement of the work of making the canal. It is said that the rent of cottages has, owing to the great detnand for residences of this class, advanced some 20 or 30 per cent, and that even at the higher rates all houses are occupied. As might be expected under the circumstances, there is some talk of building projects, and there can be little doubt that these will shortly take a practical shape. We unlerstand that the large house and grounds near Lymni Bridge, known by the name of Dane Bank, are taken by Mr. Cecil Brown, of Liverpool, who, it is said, has charge of one ot the sections of the canal. At Sta- tham and Thelwall the work of excavation is being carried forward with unabated energy, and , soon all the bends in the river in this direction will be spanned by temporary lint substantial wooden bridges. Between Morris Brook and Thelwall the two rows of navvies' huts which have been in course of erec- tion for some time past appear so far as exterior is concerned to be all but finished, though in connection with the windows there is evidently still some work for the glaziers, and no doubt the insides require many finishing touches. A new feature.in connection with the work in this locality is the laying of a line of rails toiron- nect the Thelwall length with the canal siding at Latch- fc,r4 §o,q9ul The lapne of this lino has been carried forward with characteristic exitiousness, and it seems almost complete, except at the points where it will cross Grappenhall-road, linutsford-road, and Thelwall- lane, where the continuity of the line is broken, the necessary powers and permission for intersecting the roads probably not yet having been obtained. CADISHEAD.

At the fortnightly meeting of the Barton Rural Sani- tary Authority, held on Wednesday, reference was made to the large number of plans passed for the Cadishead district, and the Surveyor to the Authority said that there was more building going on at Cadishead than in aty other part of the Authority's district. As the fUStiP•ri 1 cutting trade in this locality is very much depressed, thin must be chiefly due to the Ship Canal undertaking, 1 which has already given a great iMpettld tO trade both in Cadishead and Irlam. At a meeting of the Pendleton Finance Committee, on Monday, Mr. Alderman Bowes, who presided, read a letter from Mr. J. W. Saxon, solici- tor to the Manchester Ship Canal Company, stating that the directors of the company were much surprised that the possession of the land belonging to the committee at Cadishead required for the canal works should be re- fused, as the terms offered were very liberal and had been accepted by the Salford Corporation as to their other lands and by landowners all along the route. The directors hoped that the Pendleton Committee would re- consider their decision, and so remove the obstacle to the progress of the canal works.—The committee pissed the following resolution :—" That, the Town Clerk be in- structed to inform Mr. Saxon that this committee have no wish to place any obstacle to the progress of the Ship Canal works, but desire to be informed—and they ven- tured to ask, not unreasonably—of the intention of the company with respect to the resolution of the committee offering to them the whole of the Cadishead estate, in- cluding land and buildings, prior to the formal occupation of any portion of the land by the Canal Company.' —The price fixed by the committee is £5,060. BARTON.

• The week's progress here is very marked, though the work yet is but of a preliminary character. Two steam navvies are expected to be at work next week o one in Irwell Park and the qther at Salt Eye, and tip waggons are brought by way of the Irwell on barges. Rails are laid to the water's edge, so that the materials tan be quickly disposed of. This section of the canal is five miles long, and is under the engineering supervision of Mr. W. L. Bourke, who was until recently engaged on the Forth Bridge works, near Edinburgh.. Mr. Bourke has his office in the old corn mill at Barton aqueduct. The canal in this section will cross the existing course of the Irwell no less than eight times. Notwithstanding statements of a more or less confident character, one to the effect that a site had been selected and timber put on the land for the purpose, there is no early prospect of the 'erection of a village of huts, for the very sufficient reason that there is as yet no stint of ordinary accommodation in Eccles, Patricroft, and Barton. The model lodging-house at Patricroft is full. The contractor's district office for the present is in Peelgreen-road (formerly Darbyshire-lane), in the little old Primitive Methodist Chapel. In Salt Eve cutting, where a large body of men are at work, employment is found for two locomotives. Hitherto the wagons have been filled by hand. PROMPT RESCUE BY A GANGER.

_ A smart rescue from drowning was effected near the works at Barton the other day. A barge was ping to- wards Salford under sail, and as a man was hoisting a sail the wind blew it round, and a boy who had been holding on by it was cast overboard. Fortunately, Henry Moisten, a gauger,usppened to be near at hand with a boat. He promptly rowed to the lad's aid, and after he had sunk twice Moltson succeeded in pulling him into a boat, and thus saved his life. ACCIDENT AT NORTON.

9n Tuesday John Cook, 14 years of age, whose parents live in Ellesmere-st., Runcorn, was seriously in- jured while working on the canal at Norton. He was occupied in greasing the axles of the wheels of some waggons, when the engine that was attached was set in motion, and the wheels of several waggons went over his foot, crushing it in a fearful fashion. He was at once conveyed to Warrington Infirmary. It is said that the boy was thoughtlessly resting his foot upon the metal at the time, and that the engine driver was not aware of the boy's position. It is feared that the in- jur6l limb will have to be amputated. A TRAMP'S MIRACULOUS ESCAPE.

. A narrow escape from death occurred at Norton, on Tuesday. In the morning a tramp, who was presumably in search of work, was walking heedlessly along the bridge which spans the old quay canal, when a train of wagons came along. The buffer of the engine caught hini in the middle of the back, and sent him sprawling to the ground. After the train had passed along, some men who were at work in the locality, went to the spot, ex- pecting to have the unpleasant task of taking up the mangled remains of a human being, but they were as tonished, not only to find the man alive, but little the worse for his perilous adventure. That he had a narrow escape of being badly maimed, was evidenced by the fact that one of his clogs was completely torn from his foot. Mr. ,Grepon gave the man a dose' of

div.head: NAVVY'S STRENGTH.
div.p: A NAVVY'S STRENGTH.

As indicating a inavvy's strength, and what is expected of him, the Vicar of Nassington, the Rev. D. W. Barrett, M.A., in his'" Life and Work among the Navvies," quotes the following extract from the life of Mr. Bras- sey i—i• The. labour which a navvy performs exceeds in severity almost any other description of work—a full day's work consists of fourteen sets a day (a set is a number of waggons, in fact a train.) There are two men to a waggon. If a waggon goes out Nurteen times, each man has to seven waggons in thocourse of a day. Each waggon contains two and a quarter cubic yards. The result is that each man has to lift nearly twenty tons of earth on a shovel over his head into a waggon. The height of the lifting is about six feet. This is taking it at fourteen sets a day, but the navvies contrive to get through sixteen sets, and there are some men who will accomplish that astonishing quantity of work by three or four o'clock in the afternoon, a resnit, I believe, which is not nearly equalled by any other set of workmen in the World."

div.head: NEW BOOKS, Szc.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, Szc.

Mr. W. Paterson, of Edinburgh, publishes in three cheap, handy, and well-printed volumes the three famous works of Mr. Oliver Wendell Holmes. namely, 'The Autocrat of the Breakfast Table," " The Poet of the Breakfast Table," and "The Profes- sor at the Breakfast Table." They who have yet to read this charming series have a great treat in store; and it is scarcely too much to say that if they Tend Holmes once they will.turn to him again and again. It is possible with some voluminous writers to condense them by issuing what is termed their "Wit and Wisdom ; " but this cannot be done with the brilliant American, for his wit and wisdom are to be found in every page. It is said that Jove sometimes nods; but Holmes is always wide awake, and he keeps the reader awake too—that is if he has any capacity for intellectual stimulus. Ile has someth in g for everybody—the every-day young man. the man of science, and the poet. How delightfully he pays his tribute to the voiceless singers:— A few can touch. the magic string, • And noisy fame is proud to win them; Alas for those that never sing, But die with all their music in them! '
The three volumes, it may be adaeci,-iie---1;old singly, or together in a neat case. _ . . _

" Perils in the Transvaal and Zululand" is the title of a stirring volume from the pen of the Rev. EL C. Adams, M.A., vicar of Old Shoreham, authq, of "Who did it,'! "Who was Philip," &c. This weals happily conceived and happily carried out • there is an interesting story • which holds the whole tOgether ; but the whole embraces extraordinary adventures in South Africa, which are either strict fact or are founded on fact. A capital ac- count is given of the Zulu war; it will thrill all who read it, and particularly the young who will make themselves acquainted with historical detail while following an ex- citing story. There are numerous illustrations, and the illustrations are far above the average. The work is beautifully bound, and is printed on toned paper; it makes a capital gift book. In the "English Men of Letters" series, issued by Messrs. Macmillan and Co., we have the life of John Bunyan, as told by Mr. J. A. Froude, the historian. It is altogether a careful piece 43( writing. The reader gets a vivid picture of Bunyan and his Nvorks, while at the same time he has the advantage of the ripe scholarship and critical insight of the historian. Mr. Froucle deals with some of the myths which have gathered around Bunyan's name, and lets in upon them the light of his research. He lets the reader see the author of the "pil- grim's Progress" as a man amongst men ; and it is satis- factory to note that the more we learn of Bunyan the more he is to be admired. The "Westminster Review" for April opens with an exhaustive article on "An Equitable International Copy- right ; " and there is a critical and yet sympathetic paper on Heinrich Heine, which furnishes much infor- mation that will be new to many readers. Heine holds a unique position as a writer • his strange lauglater and tears nverflow everything. Who but he could have said —" The English loves freedom like his lawful wife, the Frenchman like a bride, the German like his old grand- mother?" Other topics dealt with in the " Review " are "Local and Imperial Taxes—who pay them ? " "The Discovery of the Solomon Islands,:' "Reminiscences of Cardinal Mazarin," " The South African Conference," &c. There is the usual reTiew of contemporary litera- ture, and of home affairs. In Scribner's Magazine we have the second and con- cluding part of "The Campaign of Waterloo." It is profusely and powerfully illustrated, and, as the subject is dealt with from a purely impartial point of view, the article is as valuable as it is interesting. There is a first paper on "The Centre of the Republic," by James Baldwin • "The Greek Verse" (illustrated) is learnedly written about by W. P. P. Longfellow; Henry M. Field contributes an article (admirably illustrated) on Gibral- tar • "A Happy Accident" is the title of a, charming finished story (also Illustrated); while the concluding paper is on "The Typewriter; its growth and uses." It should tk added that Mr. R. L. Stevenson furnishes a characteristic article; and there are several contribu- tions of high-class verse. _ _

The " Ladies"Preasury " for April is a strong num- ber. The illustrated articles include " Mentone," "Scene in.Bordighera," "Palms in the Villa"Mariaglia," and " Prince and Princess Bernadotte." There is a bright love-story called "The Transit of Venus ; " and there are instructions and information on shelling peas, needle- work, dressmaking, millinery, &c., &c.

div.head: --e-. TERRIBLE COLLIERY EXPLOSION AT
div.p: --e-. TERRIBLE COLLIERY EXPLOSION AT
WORKINGTON. TWENTY-EIGHT LIVES LOST.

A tertible..;;PlOSion--oC-Jir;eci Pit, Workington, in Cumberland, at eight o'clock on Thursday night. A blower had taken fire, and men had been engaged all day trying to extinguish it by building a wall. About eight p.m. the gas which had accumlated behind the wall exploded, and blew it down. Up to an.early hour on Friday morning five men had been .brought out dead, and three others dying. An exploring party has discovered ten or twelve more bodies. The followinghave been brought up :—Joseph Ireland, of Plimby.; William 11P(lowan, Maryport ; Tom Dixon, Seaton; John Pearson, Flimby; John Wright, Seaton. ANOTHER ACCOUNT.

The pit took fire on Thursday morning while a shot was being fired. At nine o'clock a gas blower burst out into flames and created great consterna- tion. During the whole day men were employed in endeavouring to wall off that section of the pit, and at about six o'clock they came to the top for re- freshments. The party numbered about 30. They descended the pit again, and about eight o'clock. while the managers were in the office consulting the plan of the workings so as to facilitate the work of extinguishing the fire, a loud explosion took place, which shook the whole of the buildings on the pit-top On looking out of the office the managers saw- dense volumes of smoke issuing from the pit mouth. They went to the top, and signalled down the shaft, but could get no response. They therefore proceeded to draw up the cage 'carefully, and when it reached the top they found that it contained the body of one of the workers fearfully burned. The report of the explosion had brought a crowd to the pit mouth, and several men a:: once volunteered to go down the shaft and explore the pit. Some of the offers were accepted, an at eleven o'clock they sent up the cage containing two dead bodies, and within half an hour the number of dead, dying, or injured sent to the top numbered 11. Three of the number were not very seriously hurt, three others were evidently dying, three others died in a few minutes, and the remaining two were taken to the infirmary. Some of the exploring party were very much ex- hausted by their labours. One of these was Mr. Johnstone, the manager, and another was his brother, from Aspatria. When they reached the surface they reported that they had been to the far end of the dip, and had explored the whole of the place, and had seen ten or twelve bodies lying dead.

The explosion resulted from the ignition ot a gas blower by blasting shot. A wall was being built to shut off the burning part of the mine, 'out some accumulated gas behind the wall exploded, blow- ing the wall down and killing the men behind it. Fourteen bodies were recovered by the exploring party, but about a dozen yet remain in the pit' Exploration is suspended until the pit is cleared of the foul air. RECOVERY OF BODIES.

At two o'clock on Friday morning eight of the bodies in the pit were brought up. One of them was recognised as that of Sergeant Smith, of the local Artillery Volunteer Corps. Further explora- tions on Friday morning showed that there are sti.l about a dozen bodies in the workings, but some of them had been so tor and mangled that the ex- act number could not be ascertained, and the after damp was so powerful that further operations had to be suspended. The managers have decided to flood the pit, as it has been definitely ascertained that there is nobody in the pit alive. A telegram from Workington at one p.m. on Fri- day stated that eleven bodies had been recovered, and that there are seventeen men still in the pit, the total number of victims being twenty-eight. The force of the explosion was terrific. One body was observed with the head blown off. From eight o'clock until two the gallant work of bringing up the dead and wounded continued. The bodies in

Two men were arrested in a lodging-house at Farn- worth at midnight on Tuesday, charged with attempting to murder a railway guard named Young, who was shot in the left breast—being, however, only very slightly injured—while he was walking along a road in that town on Sunday night. LOHD HAHTINGTON AT THE GUILDHALL —The Marquis of Hartington was on Wednesday invested, in the pre- sence'of a large company which had assembled at the Guildhall, with the freedom of the City. In the evening he was entertained at a banquet by the Lord Mayor at the INSan'sion House. hi the course of his speech which he delivered in response to the toast of his health as the "youngest freeman" of the City, he said that he had as a member of the Liberal party done his best to keer) up his party allegiance, but had been compelled, for a time at least, owing to the action taken by the Liberal party in regard to the Irish question, to sever his immediate connection with it.

Meetings of the Oldham cotton operatives have passed resolutions in favour of tendering a month's notice or an advance of 5 per cent, and it is believed that a refusal of the application will remit in a strike.

Cable: advices from America received to-day quote an advance of 64 per cwt. in the value of both lard and bacon. MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY.—There is a lack of force in almost every depattment of the market, and vpry little is being done. A good business has apparently been done in Liverpool without alteration of prices. Many manufacturers are wanting new business,and such offers as are now putbefore 'them are mostly of a character that leave next to nothing for working.
